articles.title: Ukraine, Russian alert systems hit with cyberattacks that spread alarming messages
articles.summary: Authorities in Ukraine and Russia say their emergency alert mobile apps were targeted by cyberattacks late Sunday, with users in Ukraine receiving false warnings of dangerously high radiation levels…

image.caption: This screenshot made on a smartphone shows a series of false alerts received late Sunday from an emergency alert mobile application that was subject to a cyberattack, in Kyiv, Ukraine. (The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

Authorities in Ukraine and Russia say their emergency alert mobile apps were targeted by cyberattacks late Sunday, with users in Ukraine receiving false warnings of dangerously high radiation levels in the capital, Kyiv.
Temporary disruption to emergency alerts featured some messages in fractured English

Authorities in Ukraine and Russia say their emergency alert mobile apps were targeted by cyberattacks on Sunday, with users in Ukraine receiving false warnings of dangerously high radiation levels in the capital, Kyiv.

In a Telegram post late Sunday, Ukraine's air raid alert channel said "unauthorized parties" had interfered with the app's operation and that the service had been temporarily suspended. It warned users not to click on links in "suspicious notifications."

Authorities in Ukraine said the app, which Ukrainians rely on to seek safety amid daily Russian missile and drone strikes, was restored overnight. The alerts — making false claims of high radiation levels, a chemical threat and public disturbances in Kyiv — were written in English with spelling and grammatical errors as well as in a mix of Russian and Ukrainian.
One of the false posts mentioned the hacking group Hitcore.
Municipal employees work in Odesa work at the site of private houses which were damaged during a Russian drone strike, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, on Monday. (Nina Liashonok/Reuters)

Mash, a Russian Telegram channel with links to the security services, said it had spoken to representatives of Hitcore and that they had claimed responsibility for the attack. That claim could not be independently verified.

Ukraine's state-run Center for Countering Disinformation reported the breach and urged users to monitor emergency channels on social media and rely on physical alerts while the cyberattack was being addressed.
Yurii Ihnat, a spokesperson for Ukraine's air force command, said the cyberattack had no impact on Ukraine's security and defence operations because the app is separate from military command systems.
Ihnat told Ukraine's private 1+1 television that the air force continues to report real-time threats through independent communication channels, including popular social media platforms.

Civilians evacuated from Russian-occupied Oleshky arrive in Ukraine-held territory

blocks.text: In Russia, officials said Monday that hackers had sent fake emergency alerts after gaining access to the Russian Emergency Ministry's mobile app.

The ministry did not name who carried out the attack. In a statement, it reassured Russians that the wider public alert system was working normally, and that the mobile app acted as a supplementary service alongside alerts shared through SMS messages, media broadcasts and municipal sirens and loudspeakers.
Limited ceasefire ends
In new fighting, Ukrainian authorities in the war-divided Kherson region reported multiple Russian drone attacks early Monday, hours after a humanitarian ceasefire expired.
The regional administration said a 62-year-old woman and a 73-year-old man were hospitalized with blast injuries in the city of Kherson, across the Dnipro River from Russian-occupied territory.
This is how residents of the besieged town of Oleshky stayed alive
The localized ceasefire ended at midnight at the start of Monday. The brief pause in fighting was tied to a humanitarian aid mission in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky.
The ceasefire, which began Oct. 27, marked the most significant truce between Kyiv and Moscow since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine began nearly five years ago.
The pause allowed besieged residents of Oleshky to be evacuated in a rare joint operation that ended Saturday.

An estimated 2,000 civilians were in Oleshky when the temporary truce took effect. They could evacuate to territory controlled by either Ukraine or Russia, or remain in the city with replenished food and medical supplies. Exact evacuation totals were withheld to protect those who stayed.
Ukraine's general staff said Monday that Russia's military had bolstered its drone defences and replenished ammunition supplies in the area during the ceasefire.
Elsewhere in Ukraine, emergency services reported that drone strikes injured 12 people in the eastern Kharkiv region and damaged a refrigeration facility, greenhouses and residential buildings.
Five people were also reported injured in the Black Sea port city of Odesa, where a warehouse was targeted and homes were damaged.

MANILA, Philippines – The International Criminal Court (ICC) will hold its fifth status conference on former Philippine president Rodrigo Duterte’s crimes against humanity case on Monday, November 2.
This comes weeks before the opening of the trial scheduled on November 30.
A status conference is where parties discuss matters related to the case before proceeding to a full trial.

So far, the court has had four conferences: on May 27, when it announced that the trial will begin on November 30; on June 23, when the chamber cautioned lawyers against granting media interviews; and the third one, on September 16, when the former president made an appearance.
The court held the fourth conference on October 13, where the parties discussed the list of evidence anew.
Duterte will skip the Monday hearing after waiving his right to be present.
For the fifth status conference, the Trial Chamber III and the parties will discuss the following:

items: Daily schedule
Audio-visual link testimony and rights of audience
List of witnesses and number of hours for the Prosecution’s presentation of evidence
Potentially exculpatory evidence, agreed facts, and calling order
Rule 68(3) applications and in-court protective measures
Security of defense missions

articles.title: ICC rejects victims' request to use Tagalog in parts of opening statement in Duterte trial
articles.summary: The International Criminal Court (ICC) Trial Chamber III that will hear the crimes against humanity charges against former President Rodrigo Duterte has rejected the counsel for the victims' request…

blocks.text: Filtered By: Topstories
News
Published November 2, 2026 6:43pm

The International Criminal Court (ICC) Trial Chamber III that will hear the crimes against humanity charges against former President Rodrigo Duterte has rejected the counsel for the victims' request that portions of their opening statement be delivered in Tagalog.

This was one of the measures that the trial chamber decided in its fifth pre-trial conference at the ICC in The Hague. Duterte was not present at the conference on Monday after the court granted the defense's request that he not attend.

Presiding Judge Joanna Korner said allowing Tagalog—which is not among the ICC’s official languages—would complicate victim applications and significantly increase trial costs because of translation requirements.
The request was raised by Public Counsel for Victims Paolina Massidda, who argued that using Tagalog was necessary to accurately convey the victims' narratives.
Massida noted that the use of Tagalog would be strictly limited to quoting victims and would not be used throughout the entire opening statement.
Under the Rome Statute, the official languages of the ICC are English and French. –NB, GMA News

articles.title: Palantir AI tech unused or little used by 29 NHS trusts said to have benefited from it
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Gap between NHS claim and trusts’ comments described as ‘very misleading’ by senior health official

More than two dozen hospital trusts the NHS claims have benefited…

blocks.text: More than two dozen hospital trusts the NHS claims have benefited from Palantir’s medical data platform are not using all or most of the AI-powered technology, the Guardian can reveal.

The 29 hospital trusts that NHS England publicly lists as “realising benefits” from the controversial £330m federated data platform (FDP) have said the system is not live or they are not using any of its applications. The apparent gap between the NHS claim and the trusts’ understanding was described as “very misleading” by one senior health official.

It comes as the health secretary, Yvette Cooper, faces calls from MPs and campaigners to axe the US tech firm’s contract to deliver the flagship government AI system, which aims to connect scattered medical files, speed up hospital discharges and improve surgery scheduling among other potentially life-saving improvements.

Palantir’s UK and Europe chief executive, Louis Mosley, said ending its contract would be “putting politics above patients” and accused critics of “Palantir Derangement Syndrome”. The company has contracts to supply AI to the Israeli military and Donald Trump’s homeland security crackdown, while its billionaire founder, Peter Thiel, has questioned democracy, said tech companies can “unilaterally change the world” and called technology an “incredible alternative to politics”.

NHS England has previously faced scrutiny over how it has used data to defend the Palantir contract, which began in 2024. It claims 117,539 more operations were carried out by trusts using the FDP in a year, but this summer it conceded it could not prove cause and effect, and the Office for Statistics Regulation (OSR) watchdog ran an investigation. Asked about the claim of NHS Trusts “realising benefits”, the OSR said it will now be “taking this forward under our casework function”.

The contrast between the number of hospitals the NHS claims realise benefits from Palantir’s technology and the statements of the hospitals themselves emerged from more than 100 freedom of information requests. NHS England states on its website that 137 trusts are “live” with the FDP, but of those described as “realising benefits”, 29 responded that they were either not using the system or its apps.

Epsom and St Helier said it was “not using FDP at the moment”, Kent and Medway said the trust “has been focused on other priorities … the FDP is not currently live”, Mersey Care said they had “not yet gone live with the FDP”, Nottingham University Hospitals said “no implementation timeline has been agreed”, and University Hospitals of North Midlands said: “FDP is not live. We do not intend to roll it out in the future.”

Chi Onwurah, chair of the Commons science and technology committee, said: “If many NHS trusts don’t see the value of the FDP, serious questions need to be asked about whether the hype surrounding Palantir’s products matches reality.”

She called on the government to activate the 2027 break clause in Palantir’s contract and launch an open competition for a UK-owned and based supplier to handle patient records. The Commons health select committee is also calling for ministers to pull Palantir’s deal.

The FOIs were obtained by Medact, a medical charity campaigning for Palantir to be ejected from the NHS, and shared with the Guardian. Medact spokesperson Dr Rhiannon Mihranian Osborne said: “Our NHS institutions are meant to work in the interests of public trust and evidence-based healthcare, not use creative accounting to justify a deeply controversial contract. There is no good reason for the government to continue this failing project. We now have to ask, if ministers are using these flawed claims to make their decision, are they being misled?”

Asked to respond, NHS England insisted nearly 140 trusts “have now reported benefits from the wide range of tools available on the platform, helping staff join up and improve care for patients, and work more efficiently.”

It has previously said that its list of hospital trusts reporting benefits includes those using the tools for back office data analysis and submission rather than to support patient care. It is understood trusts that say they do not use the FDP may use a small part of its functionality to help calculate treatment costs. For example, Torbay and South Devon NHS Foundation Trust said it is “not currently operationally using the FDP” but NHS England records it as “live” because infrastructure is in place “to support data submission, rather than active operational use of FDP apps.”

Palantir has been hitting back against criticism of its deal and last month hired Labour’s former deputy leader and member of the House of Lords Tom Watson as a full-time senior lobbyist. Watson this week has been posting videos on X aiming to debunk “myths” about Palantir, including concerns that public services will become “locked in” to its systems. He rebutted criticism from the Green party leader Zack Polanski, who said it was “beyond ridiculous” that Lord Watson was a life peer.

Watson and Mosley have also been writing directly to critical MPs in letters that have counted the times they have spoken out against the company, which one recipient, Labour’s Clive Lewis, described as “very Big Brother”.

Marc Farr, chair of the NHS Chief Data and Analytics Officers Network, said: “I am concerned to hear that there are 29 trusts reported as receiving benefits but when asked are not actually using the tool. It is great that a number of trusts that have adopted the FDP are benefiting from this nationally funded programme, but it is crucial for public support … that benefits are reported accurately, transparently and in a way that can be properly verified.”

A Palantir spokesperson said: “Palantir software is helping to deliver better care, with trusts using it recording 117,000 additional operations, a 14.3% reduction in discharge delays for long stay patients and a 5.6% improvement in the number of people finding out whether or not they have cancer within 28 days.”

articles.title: [New Rx] What if the Philippines leased an island for 100 years?
articles.summary: Hong Kong can be a model. Singapore and South Korea might bring in long-term capital, drive regional economic growth, and spark broader national governance reforms in the Philippines

blocks.text: The Philippine peso recently reached a record low of ₱64.17 against the US dollar. While currency depreciation alone does not indicate economic weakness, it raises a key question: how can the Philippines strengthen investor confidence and attract long-term capital for economic transformation?
During a visit to the Philippines, my father made an unusual suggestion: why not lease one island to another country for 100 years?

Under this proposal, the partner country would help establish a distinct legal and institutional framework while the Philippines retains sovereignty, national defense, and responsibility for essential public services. After a century, the Philippines would inherit a thriving economic center with modern infrastructure and competitive institutions.

In January 2016, then-presidential candidate Rodrigo Duterte proposed leasing islands to multinational companies with autonomy to develop infrastructure and operating rules. However, my father’s proposal differs: rather than relying on private corporations, it involves a government-to-government institutional partnership.

The historical comparison is Hong Kong. In 1898, China leased the New Territories to Britain for 99 years. Decades later, Hong Kong helped channel international capital, expertise, and commerce into Shenzhen and the Pearl River Delta, illustrating how a jurisdiction with distinct institutions can stimulate development far beyond its borders.

The Philippines already offers investment incentives and special economic zones, but these remain subject to the national administrative framework. What if one island operated under a distinct system of civil and commercial laws, an independent judiciary, taxation, and regulatory institutions?

The goal would be to offer investors predictable rules, enforceable contracts, and credible institutions. Like Hong Kong, it could feature separate residency arrangements while preserving Philippine citizenship.

Importantly, the foreign partner would not operate the entire government. The Philippines would continue providing healthcare, education, policing, municipal services, and defense. The partner would supply the institutional architecture: judicial expertise, regulatory standards, and independent oversight.

Such an arrangement would require constitutional changes, particularly to establish an independent judiciary and a distinct immigration system. The experiment would concern institutions, not merely financial incentives.

Singapore’s domestic market is small, land and labor are constrained, and its companies need international expansion. Initiatives like the Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone demonstrate its strategy of pairing financial and technological strengths with regional land and workforce capacity.

A Philippine island could offer another variation of that strategy. Singaporean businesses could establish manufacturing facilities, logistics hubs, and research campuses operating under familiar standards. Headquarters and advanced research would remain in Singapore, while land-intensive operations locate on the island.
Unlike conventional industrial parks, the arrangement would feature a separate judicial and regulatory framework supported by Singaporean institutions.

Private investors could finance much of the infrastructure, limiting Singaporean taxpayer exposure while Singapore contributes institutional expertise rather than assuming territorial administration. Singapore has not expressed interest in such an arrangement, and its potential participation would require further examination.

Alternatively, South Korea brings strengths in advanced manufacturing, engineering, and digital governance. The partner could be any country with strong institutions, proven administrative capabilities, and no territorial ambitions.

Imagine an underdeveloped island transformed into an international commercial center with modern ports, industrial parks, and universities. The benefits would extend to surrounding provinces supplying agriculture, labor, and materials, stimulating investment across the region. Any location would require an independent feasibility study and a credible process for securing the informed consent of affected communities.

To protect Philippine sovereignty, foreign military bases and territorial claims would be prohibited. The Philippines would retain national defense and natural resource rights, while existing residents’ citizenship, property rights, and political representation would be protected. Equally important, foreign partners would need assurances against unilateral termination by future Philippine administrations. A constitutionally authorized bilateral treaty, international arbitration, compensation provisions, and political-risk insurance could reduce these risks, although no legal safeguard could entirely eliminate them.

Beyond economics, experiencing predictable permits, efficient dispute resolution, and transparent rules could raise public expectations for governance across the Philippines, encouraging broader national reforms. The island’s greatest legacy might be changing what Filipinos expect from the government.

The Philippines has pursued growth through incentives and economic zones for decades. The next experiment should focus on institutional credibility. By starting with just one island, the Philippines could create a model that delivers capital, infrastructure, and institutional learning for generations to come. After 100 years, the Philippines could inherit not only a thriving economic center but also institutions and practices worth adopting elsewhere.

Speaking in Parliament in 1977 about Singapore’s need to develop its own institutional approach, then-Prime Minister Lee Kuan Yew expressed a philosophy that remains relevant far beyond its original context:
“We have got to find our own style. We have got to be bold enough to experiment.” – Rappler.com

Dr. Jaemin Park is an adjunct professor at the University of the Philippines College of Public Health and works across Southeast Asia on healthcare financing, medical innovation, and public sector reform.

articles.title: [Rappler’s Best] America, your turn
articles.summary: The US midterm elections are happening on November 3, and the results will determine control of Congress as President Donald Trump enters the last two years of his term

blocks.text: The past week thrilled liberals and leftists across the world as elections in three polarized countries stemmed the march of the far-right in Latin America, demonstrated student power in Europe, and humbled Benjamin Netanyahu.
These polls have been hard fought, but the post-election transitions will be doubly harder.

items: Crying fraud but also facing corruption charges back home, Flavio Bolsonaro, Brazil’s defeated presidential candidate, has fled to the US into the welcoming arms of his patron, US President Donald Trump. Bolsonaro can stay in America for as long as he wants, Trump said. His father, Jair, a former president, is in jail in Brazil.

Running on an anti-corruption wave, Serbia’s student protest movement managed to unseat longtime leader Aleksandar Vucic in an election, but now comes the hard part of governing. For starters, the student leaders have called for the resignation of top public officials and investigations into alleged corruption under Vucic.

In Israel, the far-right continues to dominate, but did not come out solidly for Netanyahu, whose party lost the majority in parliament. Without any bloc enjoying majority numbers, however, he will likely serve as caretaker prime minister. How could Israel break an election deadlock? Here’s an explainer.

blocks.text: And so we turn to the next logical question: what will America show the rest of the world this week?
The US midterm elections are happening on November 3, and the results will determine control of Congress as Trump enters the last two years of his term. Here are things to know.

If you’re a liberal and listened to pollster Nate Silver’s interview with Ezra Klein (as I did), you’d be expecting a “momentous” turnaround — a more than 70% chance for Democrats in the Senate — that could flip Congress against Trump. If the results reflect what he’s seeing in his polling, Silver said these would effectively end the Trump era.

The Economist has more conservative numbers. While conceding that the “auguries are good for Democrats,” it’s putting the probability of the US Senate going to the Democrats at just 54%. But the White House is already crafting a path to govern without Congress in case Democrats win, according to a Reuters report.

items: These are the races that will decide control of the US Senate, and the key seats that could shape the next House.

The campaign period has been reminiscent of traditional tactics in Philippine elections, writes Filipino-American Oscar Quiambao in this piece. There have been concerns about Republican efforts to delay the vote counts and intimidate voters. And let’s not forget that Trump himself offered $5,000 to every American if Republicans win.
There are four ways foreign policy could change if Democrats win this week.

blocks.text: This also marks the first elections in the US where voters have been relying on chatbots to guide them. It’s a cautionary tale.

items: A study showed almost 40% of chatbots’ replies to election-related queries contained at least one factual error. Read more.

The flood of AI-driven disinformation has been unprecedented, according to this story, which cites one instance when the Democrat running for US Senate in Texas (a Republican base), James Talarico, had to take time off from campaigning due to flu. A fake video about him supposedly being treated at a mental health facility in Ohio went viral.
Russia is apparently fueling fake reports about Democrats, according to an intelligence briefing that US lawmakers received. Read more.
Outside the US, in Brazil, AI content bypassed election rules — a lesson for the Philippines, writes Alex Culla in this story.

blocks.text: As Trump spent the past days doing his final push for a Republican win, his defense chief Pete Hegseth flew to Cebu for the ASEAN Defense Ministers’ Meeting. There, the host, Philippine Defense Secretary Gibo Teodoro, snubbed the Chinese defense attaché who ranked lower than him. Bea Cupin gives us a recap of the meeting in this report.
On another note, we extend our deepest condolences to the family of Philip Juico, who died on October 31 after years of battling cancer.

articles.title: Iranians have left Doha talks, draft proposal for US deal being circulated, official says
articles.summary: Iran's foreign ministry spokesperson says the basis of the talks is a seven-step plan Iran drew up in September to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and end the US naval blockade on Iran

blocks.text: Iranian negotiators have left talks with Qatari mediators aimed at ending the war with the United States, and a draft proposal is being circulated with a follow-up meeting possible, an official briefed on the talks said on Monday, November 2.
The negotiators departed on Sunday, November 1, though not because of difficulties in the negotiations, the official said, without providing further details on the draft proposal.

Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson said the basis of the talks is a seven-step plan Iran drew up in September to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and end the US naval blockade on Iran, with Tehran now suggesting that proposal could be implemented on a faster timeline under a deal.
The spokesperson, Esmaeil Baghaei, said Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi had been in Doha to facilitate the exchange of messages with Washington via Qatari intermediaries.

“Our demands have been articulated very clearly and transparently. These demands are reasonable and logical: No final agreement can be initiated, nor can the Strait of Hormuz be reopened or secured, unless the US naval blockade is brought to an end, Iran’s demands are respected, and Iran’s legitimate requirements are addressed,” Baghaei said.

On Saturday, Qatari broadcaster Al Jazeera quoted Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi as saying that under a deal the Strait of Hormuz could be opened within a two-day timeline rather than within the seven days originally envisaged.
Iran’s initial proposal was rejected by US President Donald Trump.

The latest round of diplomacy comes amid concerns that the conflict could escalate again after Tuesday’s midterm elections in the United States. Asked about Tehran’s view on the midterms, Baghaei said Tehran did not expect elections to “give birth to a new US.”
Trump has said the United States would not launch new attacks on Iran before the vote and that talks with Tehran have been productive, though he has not ruled out further military action.

articles.title: Family of murdered student Henry Nowak say police misled and manipulated them
articles.summary:
Father says family felt officers did ‘not tell the truth’ about what happened after handcuffed teenager bled to death

The family of the murdered teenager Henry Nowak, who was arrested as he…

blocks.text: The family of the murdered teenager Henry Nowak, who was arrested as he pleaded for medical help after being stabbed, have said they were failed by the authorities and fear they were manipulated in their darkest hour.

His parents described how police wrongly told them Nowak, 18, had been the aggressor, and that officers had immediately administered first aid. They said the police watchdog had initially said there was no evidence of misconduct by officers.

“The story was evolving every time we had an interaction,” Henry’s father, Mark Nowak, told ITV News. “What started off as: ‘When the police arrived, we administered first aid,’ moved through a stage where: ‘When the police arrived, they detained everyone’ … to: ‘We actually only detained Henry,’ to then: ‘We handcuffed Henry,’ and then: ‘We placed Henry under arrest.’
“That evolution of what actually happened that night really shocked us, and we felt we were being hoodwinked. We felt we were being not told the truth.”

Novak’s stepmother, Katie Nowak, said: “I do feel that we have been failed multiple times. I fear that we may have been manipulated in our darkest hours. And I fear that some decisions were made to try and protect the police and their reputation rather than help us as a family.”

The student was murdered by Vickrum Digwa, who stabbed him as he walked home from a night out in Southampton in December 2025. Nowak was handcuffed by police officers while bleeding to death after Digwa, who was eventually jailed for life, had falsely accused him of racial abuse.
In police bodyworn camera footage that prompted a public outcry, Nowak was heard repeatedly saying: “I’ve been stabbed,” to which an officer replied: “Don’t think you have, mate.”

The police watchdog, the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC), is investigating and the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, has launched a review to examine whether opportunities were missed to prevent the murder.

Speaking to ITV News, the student’s mother, Lucy Ross, said: “Henry told the police nine times that he can’t breathe, he can’t breathe and he’s been stabbed. What more do you want? Why, why’ve you just … ‘Don’t think you have mate’. What the hell is that all about? And then handcuff him. Why was Henry so dismissed and treated so badly?
“It’s bad enough losing a child. To know that then he was treated in his last moments like that. My poor little boy needed help and he didn’t get it.”

blocks.caption: Vickrum Digwa, who was sentenced to life in prison for murdering Henry Nowak. Photograph: Hampshire And Isle Of Wight Constabulary/Reuters

blocks.text: Hampshire and Isle of Wight chief constable, Alexis Boon, told ITV News: “I am incredibly sorry that in his final moments, when he needed us most, we failed him. I recognise that, for Henry’s family, this has been about more than the circumstances of one night. They have rightly raised serious concerns about the police response and their treatment throughout the investigation and since. No family should ever find themselves in this position.”

Novak’s family revealed that the IOPC had said in April: “No [Hampshire police] officers would be subject to conduct or criminal investigation. This was because there were no concerns identified in relation to officer actions.” Less than two months later, Hampshire and Isle of Wight constabulary was forced to apologise for its actions.

The police watchdog’s director of engagement, Derrick Campbell, told ITV News: “The IOPC is committed to establishing the full circumstances of this case, including whether any of the officers involved should face disciplinary proceedings, and providing Henry’s family with answers to the questions they rightly have about how the police treated Henry in the way they did on that terrible night, and why.”

articles.title: Senate majority united in stripping 2027 budget bill of ‘corruption-prone items’ – Lacson
articles.summary: Senator Ping Lacson says no one will be spared in their bid to 'cleanse' the proposed 2027 budget

blocks.text: PING LACSON. Senator Ping Lacson speaks during the Senate plenary debates on the 2026 budget on November 18, 2025.
Senate PRIB
Senator Ping Lacson says no one will be spared in their bid to 'cleanse' the proposed 2027 budget
MANILA, Philippines – The Senate majority bloc is united in removing “corruption-prone” items from the House-approved version of the proposed 2027 national budget, Senator Panfilo “Ping” Lacson said.

“The majority of senators are rallying behind Senate finance committee chairman JV Ejercito’s efforts to cleanse the 2027 budget of unwarranted, whimsical, and corruption-prone items — all means all!” Lacson said in a social media post.

Over the weekend, Lacson said Ejercito had secured the commitment of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) that it will submit all supporting documents for its infrastructure projects by Tuesday, November 3. Projects without the required documents would be removed from the House-approved version of the 2027 General Appropriations Bill (GAB).
Budget advocacy groups, including the People’s Budget Coalition (PBC) and BetterGovPH, had flagged nearly 7,000 projects worth P190 billion with no published project attachments in the HGAB.

A separate Senate review also found that the number of DPWH projects had increased from 11,420 in the National Expenditure Program (NEP) to 16,244 in the House-approved GAB. Of these, 6,271 were new projects introduced by lawmakers without prior vetting by the executive branch.
Lacson also said Ejercito would invite civil society organizations to observe the bicameral conference committee deliberations on the budget, which would be livestreamed to promote transparency.
The Senate will take up the budget bill when plenary sessions resume on November 9, with plenary debates expected to begin on November 23. – Rappler.com

articles.title: BI nabs alleged JP Dragon crime syndicate leader in Cabanatuan
articles.summary: A Japanese fugitive, reportedly among the leaders of the transnational criminal syndicate JP Dragon, was arrested during an operation in Cabanatuan City on October 31, the Bureau of Immigration (BI)…

blocks.text: Published November 2, 2026 5:36pm

A Japanese fugitive, reportedly among the leaders of the transnational criminal syndicate JP Dragon, was arrested during an operation in Cabanatuan City on October 31, the Bureau of Immigration (BI) said Sunday.

The bureau identified the Japanese citizen as 57-year-old Yamamoto Yoshitama, who is wanted in Japan for fraud, theft, and attempted theft under an arrest warrant issued by the Fukuoka Summary Court on December 27, 2022.

According to BI Fugitive Search Unit Chief Rendel Ryan Sy, Yamamoto was allegedly among the leaders of JP Dragon, a Japan-based criminal syndicate "composed largely of former yakuza members and believed to operate primarily in Metro Manila."

“The group has been linked to sophisticated telephone fraud schemes targeting elderly Japanese citizens. Its members allegedly impersonate police officers to deceive victims into surrendering their ATM cards and banking information,” BI said.
“Japanese investigators suspect that the syndicate defrauded approximately 250 victims of around ¥900 million (around Php362 million) since 2019,” it added.
Yamamoto is expected to be held at the BI Warden’s Facility while awaiting deportation proceedings.

Immigration Commissioner Joel Anthony Viado said the Philippines will not be a "safe haven" for foreign fugitives, adding that the bureau will ensure the country's borders remain secure against international criminals seeking refuge.

The BI said it remains committed to sustaining its operations against foreign fugitives and maintaining close coordination with local and international law enforcement agencies. —Lyjah Tiffany Bonzo/RF, GMA News

articles.title: US ambassador affirms 'ironclad' PH ties after controversial ASEAN defense talks
articles.summary: The United States' commitment to Philippine security is "ironclad" and Washington is "in this for the long-term," US Ambassador Lee Lipton said on Monday, November 2, weeks before US President Donald…

blocks.text: November 2, 2026 | 5:29pm
US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth leaves after attending the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Defence Ministers' Meeting in Cebu on Oct. 28, 2026.
Aaron Favila, pool via AFP

MANILA, Philippines — The United States' commitment to Philippine security is "ironclad" and Washington is "in this for the long-term," US Ambassador Lee Lipton said on Monday, November 2, weeks before US President Donald Trump is expected to stop in Manila on his way to talks with Chinese leader Xi Jinping.

Lipton's statement came days after what he described as US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's "very successful visit" to Cebu for a high-level ASEAN defense meeting, which has since become the subject of a public dispute between Manila and Beijing.
Lipton said Hegseth's "frequent engagements" with Southeast Asian partners showed the administration's "determination to strengthen alliances" and ensure "peace is backed by strength."

At the ASEAN Defense Ministers' Meeting Plus (ADMM-Plus), Hegseth proposed a US-ASEAN framework for defense cooperation and described Washington's approach in the region as "strong, quiet, and clear."

"Our commitment to Philippine security is ironclad. With President Ferdinand Marcos, Jr., the United States and the Philippines have built a powerful partnership grounded in shared principles, mutual respect, and an unwavering commitment to regional stability," Lipton's statement read.
Citing the US' continued provision of security assistance to the Philippines, among others, Lipton said: "We're in this for the long-term."

China sent only its Manila-based defense attaché to the ADMM-Plus in Cebu, its lowest-level representation since the forum began in 2010, and blamed a "self-serving" Philippine politician for blocking its participation.
The Chinese Embassy in Manila has gone a step further and accused Defense Secretary Gibo Teodoro of deliberately sending a late invitation to Beijing ahead of the defense summit.

Trump to join ASEAN summit. Trump, along with other world leaders, is expected to attend the ASEAN summit in Manila from November 16 to 18. Afterward, he will fly to Shenzhen for the APEC leaders' meeting, where he is set to hold his third meeting with Xi this year.
Hegseth said in June that the US' relations with Beijing were "better than they have been in many years."

Defense of sovereignty. Marking 45 years since the signing of the Mutual Defense Treaty, Lipton said Washington stands "firmly with the Filipino people in defending sovereignty, protecting territorial integrity, and upholding the freedom of navigation."
"We also believe our security partnership must be matched by an equally strong economic partnership," Lipton said, calling "reciprocal, mutually beneficial trade" essential.
Philippine exports have faced a 12.5% US tariff since July 24, after the US found that Manila had failed to impose and enforce a ban on imports made with forced labor.

Philippine officials have also said the two countries aim to sign a framework agreement in November under Pax Silica, a US-led initiative to build a global tech supply chain that aims to ease dependence on China.
Malacañang has declined to say whether it will be signed during Trump's visit.

articles.title: What does the Million Mask March mean for the Philippines?
articles.summary: Hacktivist activity related to the Million Mask March of a given year tends to fluctuate depending on issues brought up or simmering in the interim

blocks.text: Guy Fawkes mask image from Fauve/Wikimedia Commons
Hacktivist activity related to the Million Mask March of a given year tends to fluctuate depending on issues brought up or simmering in the interim

items: The Million Mask March, a global protest event held on November 5, originated from the hacking collective Anonymous and is associated with themes of political dissent and activism.

Past events, particularly in 2013, saw significant online defacements of Philippine government websites as a precursor to the protests, highlighting issues like political corruption and police violence.

The upcoming 2026 Million Mask March may be influenced by recent controversies within the Philippine Department of Information and Communications Technology, potentially leading to renewed protest actions.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – If you see a defaced Philippine government website this early in November, it could be a one-off event, but it also may be a single defacement of many, owing to a movement called the Million Mask March.

The Million Mask March is a worldwide day of protest held on November 5 and is also colloquially known as “Operation Vendetta,” after the movie and British graphic novel V for Vendetta, wherein the main character of the story wears a Guy Fawkes mask.

Originally set up by hacking collective Anonymous, the Million Mask March began in 2012 with the largest events occurring outside the Philippines, such as in London in the United Kingdom and Washington DC in the United States.

The event is usually preceded by hacking activities or online defacements of websites to drum up interest and sentiment in conducting a Million Mask March in a given locality. These defacements and hacks decry a number of issues, such as political corruption, police violence and militarization.
This was most strongly felt in the early iterations of the protest, especially in the Philippines’ 2013 Million Mask March, which saw more than 30 Philippine government websites crashed or defaced.

A video from Anonymous on the affected sites back then apologized for the disruption but called on citizens to join the November 5 protest action. In response, police at the time also took steps to maintain public safety, but also invited protesters in for questioning.
Activity related to Million Mask March tends to fluctuate depending on the time frame of issues brought up.

While the 2025 Million Mask March was apparently less pronounced and did not receive as much media coverage save for notices in online hacking communities, there’s no telling what might spur on a 2026 protest action.

The Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT) could possibly be in for a long few days of work though, seeing as there is a new DICT secretary, former Social Security System chief Robert Joseph de Claro,.

There also seeming loss of trust in the institution owing to the actions — and resignation — of the previous DICT secretary, Henry Aguda, as regards the temporary banning of Discord and the threat to ban other services that may be responsible for the spread of nihilistic violent extremism.

There’s also the preventive suspension of DICT eGov Undersecretary David Almirol over alleged conflicts of interest in the eGov app and the system’s development, which may bring an opportunity for bad actors or hacker-activists to take advantage of the situation.

blocks.caption: Conflict of interest? Audit questions DICT usec’s ties to former company Multisys

blocks.text: Unfortunately, there’s no telling what could spark strong protest actions on November 5 in the Philippines, and it’s just as difficult to determine if an informal Million Mask March is coming this year.
Perhaps it’s better to remember the fifth of November as a day when plans to bring injustices to the forefront of public consciousness comes to a head.
Though in this country, that may as well be any given weekday. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Burnham declines to say net migration still too high as Mahmood prepares to unveil tougher settlement rules – UK politics live
articles.summary:
Home secretary to make some migrants wait 10 years or more for right to settle in UK

Good morning. Often these days, when the government has a big announcement and just before the relevant…

blocks.text: Good morning. Often these days, when the government has a big announcement and just before the relevant minister starts to give the details in a statement to MPs, Lindsay Hoyle, the Commons speaker, erupts with fury and rants and raves at the Treasury bench about how all the main points have already been leaked to the media, in contravention of the ministerial code.

Not today. Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, will this afternoon unveil the final version of her plans to make foreign workers wait longer before they can apply for indefinite leave to remain, and we know relatively little about what she will say. The original plans were unveiled last November and they would require most workers to wait 10 years, not five, for ILR, with care workers having to wait 15 years. They would also apply to foreign workers already here, not just new arrivals. These proposals were hugely controversial, and Andy Burnham himself was among the ministers arguing that care workers should be treated more kindly.
As Jessica Elgot and Chris Osuh report in our overnight story, there has been some sort of climbdown in relation to care workers.
But it also seems to be the case that the broad thrust of the plan is being retained and that ILR rules are being toughened in a way that will affect hundreds of thousands of people.

The detail, which is coming after 3.30pm, will be crucial; so will the reaction of Labour MPs. When Mahmood announced these plans last autumn, some government backbenchers were horrified. But mostly public condemnation was muted. At the time Reform UK had a lead of more than 10 points over Labour in the polls and Mahmood – who was arguing that net migration was too high and that low-skilled foreign workers ended up being a burden on the taxpayer (a key Reform UK claim, although one contested by experts) – was pushing at an open door.
Now the situation is very different. The electoral threat from Nigel Farage has receded quite a lot. And net migration is falling like a stone. Here are the figures from last week’s OBR report.

blocks.caption: Net migration figures Photograph: OBR

blocks.text: To implement the ILR changes, Mahmood does not need primary legislation and that means there will be no chance for potential Labour rebels to amend the plans in the Commons. But it has been reported that more than 100 MPs are queasy about what is being planned.

And Andy Burnham himself has accepted that the context has changed. We won’t hear from him until much later, because he is spending most of the day on a flight to the Commonwealth summit. But, in an interview for an ITV documentary being broadcast tomorrow, he declined to say that net migration was too high. When Keir Starmer was PM, he regularly did say this, and that he wanted immigration to fall “significantly”. Burnham told ITV small boat crossing numbers were “too high, for certain”. However, asked about legal migration, he replied:

double quotation markIt’s come right down. And I think when you have planned migration, it’s difficult to say is it too high or too low, because it’s got to be, if you like, following gaps in the economy.
Burnham said legal migration had “come right down”. He declined to be drawn on whether it had to come down further.

This means that Mahmood will today be defending plans drawn up in response to a problem that some might argue no longer exists. However, speaking in the Commons last November, Mahmood argued she had to do something about the “so-called Boriswave, specifically the cohort of lower-qualified workers who – along with their dependants – entered the country through the health and care visa” because some of them were “never expected to be net economic contributors”, making “more stringent” controls needed.
Here is the agenda for the day.
11.30am: Downing Street holds a lobby briefing.
12.30pm: Danny Kruger, Reform UK’s head of government preparations, gives a speech to the Policy Exchange thinktank.
2.30pm: Angela Rayner, the housing secretary, takes questions in the Commons.
After 3.30pm: Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, gives her statement on the changes to indefinite leave to remain rules.
Evening: Andy Burnham arrives in Antigua for the Commonwealth summit.

Also, at some point today Labour will give an update on how many power-sharing agreements at council level with Greens will continue, in the light of Labour HQ saying recently Labour councillors should only continue to work with local Green parties willing to disown the “Zionism is racism” motion passed at the Green conference.

I’m afraid we are no longer able to have comments open below the line every day on this blog. If you want to contact me, please email politics.live@theguardian.com. You can use this email to flag up corrections, comments for publication, questions or complaints.

articles.title: John Leeson, voice behind Doctor Who’s K9, dies at 83
articles.summary:
Actor, who appeared in Dad’s Army and Rainbow, remembered as ‘true gent’ by TV producer Russell T Davies

John Leeson, the actor best known as the voice of K9, the robot dog in Doctor Who,…

blocks.text: John Leeson, the actor best known as the voice of K9, the robot dog in Doctor Who, has died at 83.
Leeson’s son, Guy Ducker, shared the news on Facebook. He wrote: “I regret to announce the death of my father … after a summer of illness. The end was peaceful.”
In a separate post on social media, Ducker said: “Many thanks to the Whovian community for the love they showed to my father over the decades, it meant a lot to him and me.”

Born John Ducker in 1943, he trained at Rada before embarking on a successful career on stage and screen. He was known for his character work across a range of TV shows such as Dad’s Army, Sorry!, Crown Court and Longitude, while other credits included The Bill, Vanity Fair, Doctors and Blake’s 7. He was also a continuity announcer on Channel 4.
But Leeson was best known for K9, created by Bob Baker and Dave Martin, who was introduced to Doctor Who in 1977 in a Tom Baker-led story called The Invisible Enemy.

Originally only intended to appear in that single script, the production team believed the character would be popular with younger viewers, and decided to have the metallic mutt join the Tardis team. He stayed until 1981 – although K9 was also voiced for a period by David Brierly – establishing the catchphrase “Affirmative, Master” when addressing the Doctor.

blocks.caption: Leeson with wife Judy Griffiths on their wedding day in 1969. Photograph: Gary Weaser/Getty Images
K9 flanked by the stars of Doctor Who in 1993. Photograph: Maximum Film/Alamy
Leeson standing amid an ITV audience in 1993. Photograph: ITV/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Leeson reprised the role in the 20th anniversary special of Doctor Who and in a spin-off K-9 and Company, which featured Elisabeth Sladen as popular companion Sarah Jane Smith. Sladen and Leeson were reunited in Doctor Who in 2006 in a David Tennant episode called School Reunion, before featuring in the CBBC spin-off Sarah Jane Adventures, which aired from 2007 until Sladen’s death in 2011.

In an Instagram post after Leeson’s death, the former Doctor Who showrunner Russell T Davies said: “There was no question that we’d ask John to provide the voice” when the robot returned. “A posh dog, uppity, haughty, wry, but somehow innocent too, and so funny. Pitched perfectly so that kids could impersonate him. That’s not easy. A true gent, and a great loss.”

Keith Barnfather, who first worked with Leeson in the 1980s and who produces behind-the-scenes documentaries about Doctor Who, described the actor as “kind, considerate, professional, charming, talented, unassuming”. Lisa Bowerman, who has credits for work across the Doctor Who universe, remembered him as “an utterly lovely man, excellent company and – and I don’t hesitate to use this word for once – a truly iconic voice”.

After leaving school, Leeson worked as a hospital porter before auditioning for Rada. Talking about his career in interviews, Leeson described it as being in two parts: “Half of my career has been pretty much as a stage actor and the television half of my career arose pretty much by accident.”

blocks.caption: The stars of Rainbow, from left: Bungle, Zippy, George and Geoffrey Hayes. Leeson said he felt ‘really ill inside this bear suit’. Photograph: Rex/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Leeson had a stint playing Bungle on the children’s show Rainbow, a job in which he described being “poured out of this costume every evening into a taxi”, because a day’s work in a small studio under the hot lights left him “really ill inside this bear suit”.

He also once lamented the haircut he was given when appearing on Dad’s Army, saying: “I was livid because they gave me an army haircut, a real basin job, and then of course put me in a balaclava and a tin hat, so nobody could see the hair anyway.”

He was still working as K9, providing voices for Big Finish audio dramas last year. This was despite, he once said, being told by producers at the BBC after his debut that “under no circumstances would there be anything after the first episode has been shot and is in the can. So don’t expect too much. And here I am in 2025 still attached to Doctor Who … I got to meet a tremendous number of knees doing K9.”

articles.title: Ryanair considers pay freezes and reducing crew on flights as fuel costs soar
articles.summary:
Airline also weighs up increasing use of AI as part of cost-cutting measures to offset impact of Iran war

Ryanair is considering cost-cutting measures including implementing pay freezes,…

blocks.text: Ryanair is considering cost-cutting measures including implementing pay freezes, reducing crew on flights and increasing the use of AI to offset soaring fuel costs because of the Middle East conflict.

Europe’s biggest low-cost carrier said it expects European airlines to raise their ticket prices by as much as 20%, as it anticipates its jet fuel costs will increase by about €2bn (£1.6bn) in its next financial year, which ends in March 2028.

“Unless there is a swift resolution of the Middle East conflict we expect jet fuel prices to remain elevated well into 2027,” said Michael O’Leary, the chief executive of Ryanair. “While we believe European short-haul fares will increase materially to reflect these much higher jet-fuel prices and competitor capacity reductions, this is unlikely to provide a full offset for an estimated €2bn increase in our fuel bill.”
The oil price hit a six-month high last Friday but fell on Monday to about $110 a barrel.
Ryanair said it expects European short-haul fares will “increase materially” next year as a result, as the oil hedging deals taken out by airlines to reduce costs come to an end.

“To help address this, we’re reviewing all costs across group airlines with a particular focus on airport churn negotiations, maturing labour agreements (which may require temporary pay freezes), lower crew ratios and increased use of AI,” O’Leary said.
The company said the AI drive would be focused on “further operational and back office/support functions” productivity.
Ryanair said its fuel requirements through to the end of March remain 80% hedged at $67 a barrel.
The company’s hedges for the following 12 months are 25% hedged at $95 a barrel.

The Irish airline, Europe’s largest in terms of passenger numbers, said that average fares fell by 2% year on year in the quarter to the end of September. Ryanair added that fare prices in the final three months of the year were trending “modestly ahead” of the same quarter last year.

“The booking window remains closer-in which reduces visibility,” the company said.“[The current quarter’s] fare outcome will heavily depend on the strength of close-in October-November school midterm [holiday] and Christmas bookings.”

The airline reported a post-tax profit of €1.61bn in the quarter to the end of September, a fall of 6% year on year but in line with analyst expectations. Passenger numbers grew 5% year on year to 64.5 million for the quarter.

articles.title: Who’s coddling Bato dela Rosa? Not us, says MNLF
articles.summary: The Moro National Liberation Front quickly distances itself from the fugitive senator, after Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla said Dela Rosa is being protected by an 'armed group' in Mindanao

blocks.text: BATO. Senator Ronald 'Bato' dela Rosa attends the Senate plenary session on May 12, 2026.
The Moro National Liberation Front quickly distances itself from the fugitive senator, after Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla said Dela Rosa is being protected by an 'armed group' in Mindanao
If Senator Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa is, indeed, hiding in Mindanao, the Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF) insists they’re not the ones sheltering him.

In a statement, the MNLF denied it is the “powerful armed group” that had been “cuddling” (or shouldn’t that be coddling?) Dela Rosa, who is wanted by the International Criminal Court (ICC) over his alleged role in the bloody drug war of the Rodrigo Duterte administration.
“The MNLF is not cuddling Senator Bato. There is no established formal relationship between Sen. Ronald ‘Bato’ dela Rosa and the MNLF,” the group said in its statement.
Dela Rosa has been out of public view since May amid the ICC arrest warrant.
The MNLF made the statement after Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla said that he had received information that the legislator was being protected by an “armed” group in Mindanao.
Remulla had also warned that attempting a forced arrest on the lawmaker could cost “10,000” lives, to explain why he would rather negotiate the senator’s surrender.

The interior chief did not identify the alleged armed group. The MNLF, however, was quick to distance itself from the speculation, saying the personal ties between former president Rodrigo Duterte and MNLF founder Nur Misuari should not be construed as evidence that the group was hiding dela Rosa.

“The claim that the MNLF may be protecting him is speculation, not a confirmed fact. Reports emphasize that the MNLF is fragmented and that it is uncertain whether the Misuari faction would-or could-shield him from arrest,” the group said.

“So, the accurate answer is: dela Rosa appears to have personal and political connections to figures associated with the MNLF, especially through Duterte’s relationship with Nur Misuari, but there is no verified evidence that he is an MNLF member, ally in an operational sense, or currently being protected by the group,” it added.

Partido Demokratiko Pilipino Lakas ng Bayan, Dela Rosa’s political party, has appealed to the Supreme Court for a swift resolution of Dela Rosa’s case. The senator’s camp also urged the High Court to reverse its earlier ruling and stop the use of an ICC warrant of arrest against him.
But with the senator still nowhere to be found, could his arrest be drawing closer?
The Philippine National Police has intensified its manhunt for its former chief after the one-week deadline for his voluntary surrender lapsed.
Senator Panfilo “Ping” Lacson, who previously called for Dela Rosa’s safe arrest, has a reminder for authorities: Keep their operations under wraps.

“When pursuing a high-profile target or handling a sensitive live case, secrecy discipline is key — unless disinformation is necessary to flush the quarry into the open,” Lacson, a former PNP chief, said in a social media post.
Did Lacson have anyone in particular in mind when he gave the unsolicited advice? – Rappler.com

articles.title: Canada had more than 220 gambler suicides in last decade — but no inquests
articles.byline: Dave Seglins, Saloni Bhugra, Andreas Wesley

image.caption: As gambling expands in Canada, experts call on coroners to do a better job of investigating and tracking gambling related deaths. (Julien de Rosa/AFP/Getty Images)

blocks.text: This story is part of a CBC News series examining the public health impacts of online gambling.
Dave, a retiree recovering from gambling addiction, says that when he was winning, he felt like a king, hooked by the prospect of wealth and recognition.
But he says like most gamblers, he "inevitably" started losing.

"Not only money — trust, people we care for, spouses, children, we lose the whole gamut. Everything that we built goes crumbling down," he told CBC News during a recent online Gamblers Anonymous meeting in Toronto.
"So we often try suicide, which I did try. I turned out to be an utter failure at that."
CBC reporter Dave Seglins speaks to a Gamblers Anonymous meeting in Toronto. (Ousama Abdel Rahman/CBC)
A CBC News investigation has found that at least 220 problem gamblers in Canada have died by suicide in the last decade, which includes a tripling of gambling-related suicides in Ontario since 2022.

items: Ontario sees surge in gambling addiction, suicides after expansion

blocks.text: But the national numbers are likely higher, as Alberta, Saskatchewan, Nova Scotia, Yukon and Nunavut don’t track gambling-related deaths, citing a lack of obvious indicators in most death investigations.

What’s more, no coroner in Canada has ever held an inquest into the issue — unlike in Australia and the United Kingdom, where inquests are being used to critically examine the gambling industry and the links between addiction and suicide.
'Misery and great harm'
A coroner in Australia delivered a scathing inquest report last month, calling for major industry reforms after investigating the suicide of 22-year-old Kyle Hudson.
Hudson opened online betting accounts after his 18th birthday and over four years, placed more than 10,000 bets, losing a cumulative $47,000 Cdn.
The morning he died, he had placed and lost bets worth $6,200.
Coroner Paul Lowrie concluded that Hudson’s preferred platform, SportsBet, ought to have detected his problem gambling.

"Kyle’s case reveals, in the sharpest relief, the human cost of online gambling," the coroner wrote. "It should be a clear signal that we cannot leave monitoring and intervention solely in the hands of the betting companies."
Kyle Hudson was 'a young man brimming with promise,' according to a coroner's report in Australia. He was working part-time while in his fourth year at university and loved sport. (ABC.net.au)
Hudson’s betting escalated and triggered 37 alerts on SportBet’s internal "Safer Gambling" monitoring system, the inquest heard.
The company sent him automated support emails and on multiple occasions called him to suspend his account, only to receive a call back from Hudson, who convinced them to reinstate it.
SportsBet also sent Hudson hundreds of bonus offers and inducements to continue playing, which the coroner found to be "contrary" to the company’s safer gambling programs.
"These products are carefully designed to keep gamblers engaged and active, and to extract net losses over time," Lowrie wrote.
"They are dangerous and capable of causing misery and great harm, especially for the young or those whose traits may make them more vulnerable."
SportsBet maintained during the inquest that Hudson did not have a gambling problem. That’s despite accounts from Hudson’s family, experts and analysis of the extent of his online gambling activity.
"It is chilling that this is SportsBet’s view," Lowrie concluded.
LISTEN | The Big Bet:
Understood: The Big Bet2:32Introducing The Big Bet
Inquests examine gambling companies' player data
Charles Ritchie of Sheffield, England, who started the charity Gambling With Lives, says inquests are an important tool to change laws and cast light on the gambling industry.
He became an advocate after his 24-year-old son Jack took his own life in November 2017.

"We realized straight away that it was gambling that had killed him. It was there in his suicide note," Ritchie told CBC News, detailing how Jack had started gambling as a teen and got hooked online after a fluke win of 1,000 pounds ($1,870 Cdn) on an electronic gaming terminal.
Jack Ritchie’s online gambling addiction led to his death, a U.K. coroner found. (Leigh Day law firm)
Ritchie says an inquest into Jack’s death in 2022 validated that it was caused by gambling.
Beyond that, he says inquests have become a valuable tool for grieving families to hold companies accountable if they have failed to intervene in cases of addiction.
Gambling apps can spot warning signs, says watchdog
After someone’s death, he says inquests can analyze the deceased’s behaviour using player data and banking records.

"When we look at those figures in the raw… Somebody is, at four o'clock in the morning, having hundreds of bets, is losing hundreds of pounds. You as a human being would say, ‘This is wrong. We need to intervene,’" he said.
"Gambling companies don't do that. And that has been found in so many of the inquests."
The U.K. has held inquests into the gambling deaths of, clockwise from top left, Arthur Soames, Jack Ritchie, Oliver Long, Gareth Evans, Luke Ashton, Ellen Mulvey and Lee Adams. (Leigh Day law firm)
No inquests in Canada
The U.K. has held seven gambling-related inquests since Jack Ritchie’s death inquiry in 2022, resulting in numerous recommendations to the government and the gambling industry.
Coroners and medical examiners in Canada have never undertaken a similar investigation.
CBC contacted chief coroners and medical examiners across Canada, who acknowledge not every jurisdiction tracks gambling suicides.
Nor do most coroners consider whether problem gambling was a contributing factor during suicide investigations. It can be hard to detect without an explicit suicide note.

People with gambling addictions tend to hide their problem from family and friends. Coroners don’t routinely probe a suicide victim’s financial records or online history to determine whether they had a gambling problem.
Journalist Rob Csernyik, author of A Losing Hand: The Human Cost of Canada’s Gambling Epidemic, says chief coroners pledged in 2003 to begin tracking the problem nationally. It has never happened.
"It's just something that hasn't been on the radar in many years in Canada, despite the expansion of gambling," Csernyik told CBC News.
Canada lacks data on gambling suicides, despite the expansion of online betting, says author and journalist Rob Csernyik. (Roger Cosman/CBC)
"I think that now with the larger push into legal gambling markets, that it's something we finally need to address."
Dr. Shawn Kelly says the tripling of gambling-related suicides in Ontario since 2022, the year the province legalized private online betting, worries him that we'll see an epidemic of addiction.
"This is the thing I’ve been fearful for," said Kelly, an adolescent addiction specialist in Ottawa.
He’s calling for much closer monitoring of problem gambling as well as restrictions on gambling advertising to curb gambling’s harms before they get worse.
"To me, it would be much too late to act when we had irrefutable evidence that our changes in gambling legislation have led to an increase in suicide amongst the vulnerable."
Dr. Shawn Kelly says the tripling of gambling-related suicides in Ontario since 2022 is a warning sign for public health officials. (Ousama Farag/CBC)
CBC asked Ontario’s Ministry of Health to comment on the rise in gambling addiction and related suicides in the province.
The minister’s press secretary deferred to Ontario’s Ministry of Tourism, Culture and Gaming, which oversees the province’s $3-billion-a-year online gambling market.

The Gaming Ministry did not address the rise in suicide rates but said in an email that since 2018, "our government has invested $421 million, including $70.1 million over the last year, in responsible gambling education, research and addiction treatment."
In the meantime, members at Gamblers Anonymous, a peer-to-peer support group with chapters around the world, are hoping more people who are struggling reach out for help.
Dan, who like Dave considered suicide, describes the group as a "big extended family."

"If I didn't find GA (Gamblers Anonymous), there's a very solid chance that either I'd be living on the streets, lost my home, marriage or even dead," he told CBC News. "That came across my mind many times."
Gamblers Anonymous 'saved my life,' says recovering gambler
Are you, or someone you know, suffering from gambling? Support is available.

articles.title: Economic frustration set to boil over in midterm elections
articles.summary: The U.S. economy is booming. But American consumers have never been more pessimistic. Economists blame tariffs and the war with Iran.

image.caption: U.S. President Donald Trump dances during a campaign rally at Rock Hill Sports and Event Center, on Thursday, in Rock Hill, S.C. (Scott Kinser/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Business·Analysis
The U.S. economy is booming. But American consumers have never been more pessimistic. Economists blame tariffs and the war with Iran.
Consumer sentiment hits all-time low as Americans head to the polls
American voters are headed to the polls for the U.S. midterms this week. Most are angry and frustrated about the state of the economy and the way Donald Trump has managed it.
If you want evidence of that dissatisfaction look no further than the University of Michigan's Index of Consumer Sentiment.
It shows consumer confidence is plummetting under Trump.

"Only three times since the 1970s have more than half of Americans said their government's doing bad job managing the economy. Right now it's at 74 per cent," said Kathryn Anne Edwards, a labour economist and policy consultant in Houston.
The index gauges consumer sentiment. It is lower today than it was during the toughest recessions in the 1980s or even the financial crisis in 2008-09.
And she says that survey is one of the biggest and longest standing bodies of economic data in the country. It's been going on since the 1940s. And it's been a monthly survey since 1978.
Edwards says these kinds of numbers show that on some fundamental level, the U.S. economy is failing American households.
"It's so completely unprecedented. It's really hard to put into words," said Edwards.
Those kind of plunges in consumer sentiment historically only happen in the deepest and darkest days of a recession.
And that's what's odd.
The U.S. economy is nowhere near a recession.
The latest GDP numbers out of Washington show the U.S. economy is the fastest growing economy in the Western world.
American GDP expanded by 3.8 per cent in the quarter running from July to September. (By comparison, Canada is on track for about a third of that growth.)
Retail sales were up. Investment in AI continues to churn ever higher. And stock markets are at an all-time high.

"GDP is growing above trend, consumer spending remains robust, layoffs trudge along at ultra-low levels, and we've seen a stable unemployment rate over the past year," wrote RBC's team of economists Mike Reid, Carrie Freestone and Imri Haggin.
But if the macro data is so good, why are voters so angry?

"For many voters, the economy is now synonymous with inflation, as rising prices outweigh job reports, housing affordability and stock market performance," wrote Francis Généreux, lead economist at Desjardins Group in a note to clients.
And those rising prices have been driven by two main things; tariffs and the U.S.-led war with Iran.

Gas prices shot up the day the war began. They have bounced around a little as talk of various ceasefires and deals come and go, but American drivers are paying far more at the pumps today than they were a year ago.
And gasoline prices are posted everywhere as drivers and pedestrians alike move through a neighbourhood. So even if you ride a bicycle to work, the increase in prices is incredibly hard to ignore.
Inflation in the U.S. has ticked up to 3.7 per cent, and economists warn it's not done climbing yet.
Yes, much of that increase is due to energy costs. But tariffs have contributed as well.
A recent report from the New York Federal Reserve found the cost of many everyday items would have declined last year were it not for Trump's tariffs.
Researchers looked at the 12-month change in consumer goods prices going back to the peak of the COVID-era surge in inflation. They showed price growth was still falling in 2024 and reversed in 2025.

"Our estimates attribute this increase to the tariffs: by February 2026, tariffs had contributed 2.9 percentage points to goods price inflation, and without them goods prices would have fallen slightly," wrote Mary Amiti, Sebastian Heise and David E. Weinstein.

And Edwards says voters have followed the Trump administration's policy decisions and how they drive prices. She says there are two sharp drops in the consumer sentiment index. One when tariffs were introduced and the other when the war with Iran began.
"Americans get it. Tariffs have made their lives more expensive," she said.

And Americans will take that knowledge into the polling booth this week. If the polls hold, the midterms could lead to sweeping changes in the formation of Congress and who holds power on Capitol Hill.
But whether those newly elected Senate and House members actually take action to lower tariffs for Canadians is a different question altogether.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Peter Armstrong is the CBC's senior business correspondent. He was a foreign correspondent and a parliamentary reporter for CBC News. Peter hosted the business program On the Money and World Report on CBC Radio. He is the author of the CBC newsletter Mind Your Business
