articles.title: Minns warns expected RBA rate rise will see ‘shops close that don’t reopen’ as pressure mounts on PM
articles.summary:
Frustration grows over the economy with one Labor MP saying voter anger is already high ahead of Reserve Bank of Australia decision

  • Get our

blocks.text: The NSW premier, Chris Minns, has warned an expected interest rate increase will force job losses and cause businesses to close, insisting the federal government and states should rein in spending to take pressure off the economy.
The intervention from the leader of the country’s biggest state will heap yet more pressure on the Albanese government ahead of the Reserve Bank of Australia’s cash rate decision on Tuesday.
Markets predict the bank will deliver the fifth rate rise in 2026. A move to 4.85% would bring rates to their highest level in 18 years.
Minns, who is increasingly outspoken on differences of opinion with the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, said increasing rates was not “a straightforward decision” for the RBA.
“The impact of another rate rise on the New South Wales economy will be massive,” Minns said.
“There’ll be jobs that go that will never come back. There’ll be shops that close that do not reopen with another rate rise.
“We can’t be flippant about this, this is a very, very tough call for them.”
Asked about government spending adding to inflation pressure, Minns said: “I think everybody needs to do their bit.”

Albanese and the treasurer, Jim Chalmers, have confirmed next month’s mid-year budget update will including a savings package, even as they point to international factors including the war in Iran as the cause of price hikes.
Internally, frustration is growing about the government’s handling of the economy.
One Labor MP told Guardian Australia voter anger was already high ahead of the rates decision, likening the tough political climate facing the government during a slump in polling in its first term.

They said Albanese and Chalmers would be hoping the trajectory for inflation and interest rates experienced before the 2025 election would play out again next year. After peaking at nearly 8% in late 2022, inflation fell to within the Reserve Bank’s target band before voters went to the polls.
“It’s the mid point in the cycle and people are grumpy,” the MP said.
Albanese will be at the commonwealth leaders’ summit in Antigua and Barbuda on Tuesday when the RBA announces its rates decision, leaving Chalmers to speak for the government.
The environment minister, Murray Watt, defended the government’s spending on Monday.
“We need to remember that Australia is not the only country going through inflationary pressures at the moment,” he told ABC radio.
“This is a global phenomenon, and even if the Australian government was to cut its budget to zero, we would still be experiencing inflationary pressures because of what’s happening around the world.”
after newsletter promotion
Labor frontbencher Tanya Plibersek defended Chalmers, insisting the savings would be meaningful but would not hurt households.
“There’s been no reforming treasurer in Australian history that hasn’t copped it when they’ve made big changes,” Plibersek said. “We all support Jim.”

blocks.caption: Inflation is ‘too high’, but RBA says Australia is not heading for recession – video

blocks.text: The ACTU secretary, Melissa Donnelly, warned workers “cannot survive another interest rate rise”, in a demonstration outside the RBA’s Sydney headquarters. She blamed big banks and supermarket giants for adding to the pressure on households by slugging customers.

“Workers are already struggling and feeling the brunt of these cost-of-living pressures. Workers didn’t create this inflationary crisis, it’s caused by Trump’s war in the Middle East, but workers are feeling the pain of it every day,” she said.

The Australian Council of Social Service chief executive, Cassandra Goldie, urged the RBA not to increase interest rates, calling instead for action to lower housing and energy prices and out of pocket medical costs.
“Higher interest rates create unemployment by design,” she said.

“We cannot be certain what the impact of another rate hike now will be on unemployment in a year’s time. An increase towards or above 5% would be disastrous, locking people out of jobs for years and forcing them to rely on grossly inadequate income support payments.”
Monday’s Newspoll put Labor’s primary vote at 27%, behind One Nation on 28%, but remaining ahead of the Coalition on 21%.
The opposition leader, Angus Taylor, accused the federal government of losing control of inflation and interest rates.
“We’re seeing a Labor government that can’t control its spending,” he said. “It cannot control its spending and the result of that is the Reserve Bank needs to do all the hard work.”

articles.title: Iran killed her teenage daughter - now she is facing up to the regime
articles.summary: Samira's 16-year-old daughter Sevda was shot dead as they took part in mass protests in January.

blocks.text: Warning: Distressing content and strong language
Samira says she never used to be political.
"I worked in sales in Iran. I sold cosmetics," she tells BBC Panorama.

But that all changed the day her only child was shot dead in front of her by Iranian security forces. Sixteen-year-old Sevda was taking part in protests against Iran's repressive regime that engulfed the country earlier this year - before the US and Israel launched widespread air strikes which killed the country's supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
Samira's grief became fury as Iran's authorities then hindered, rather than helped, her search for her daughter's body, she says.
"I realised that finding Sevda wasn't the end, but just the beginning of all the harassment they put me through."
Samira made a dramatic escape from Iran on foot, navigating dangerous mountainous terrain.

She now lives abroad in hiding, describing herself as a "one-woman army fighting the regime". In a search for accountability and justice after her daughter's death, she is intent on naming the members of the security forces and officials she believes were responsible for firing fatal shots during the protests.
"They'll bring me to the brink of death before they kill me, but finding me won't be easy… Return to normal life? There is no going back," she says.

Samira is among several Iranians the BBC has spoken to since the start of the year. Some, still inside the country, told Panorama they wanted to speak out despite the risks, saying they had found it difficult to hold on to hope once the mass protests had been brutally crushed.

The Iranian embassy in London told Panorama that peaceful and legitimate protests had been hijacked by foreign powers, including the US, which promoted violence, provided weapons and equipment, and compromised public security.

Sevda was killed on 9 January as she and Samira took part in huge demonstrations on the outskirts of the capital Tehran which had begun the previous month. They had been sparked by economic discontent, before escalating into calls for an end to the country's Islamic Republic.

Though Samira denies she was especially political then, she says her daughter was. Sevda's idols were two other young women - Mahsa Amini, whose death in custody after an alleged violation against the mandatory headscarf triggered mass protests, and Nika Shakarami, who was killed during a subsequent uprising against Iran's strict Islamic dress code for women.
"She kept them alive in her thoughts and always wanted to continue their path [of resistance]," Samira says.

The day before Sevda was killed, the numbers protesting had been particularly high. Samira says she and Sevda had responded to a call by Reza Pahlavi, the exiled son of Iran's last shah (king), for demonstrations.
"The security forces had lost control," she says.
The swell in numbers had spooked Iran's government, and the following day a shoot-to-kill order was announced, Samira says. But she had thought it just an empty threat.
"They lied so much in Iran… We couldn't imagine a massacre of that scale."
And they were reassured, she says, by US President Trump's promise that he had their backs.
He had told US media on 8 January: "I have let [the Iranian authorities] know that if they start killing people, which they tend to do during their riots… we're going to hit them very hard."
But nevertheless the crowds appeared smaller on the 9th, Samira says.
Sevda seemed to know the risks, she says. Her daughter took off her earrings and gave them to her grandmother. She also shared her phone passcode with Samira.
The mother and daughter gathered with the rest of the protesters. Sevda then stood on a dustbin and began leading a chant.

"It seemed there were more forces than people," Samira says of the area where they were. "I don't know how, within one day, they gathered so many… Basijis and IRGC [Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps] forces."
The IRGC defends the country's Islamic establishment, and the paramilitary Basij Resistance Force are volunteers for the IRGC.

"A sniper fired from the roof of a building on our right. The bullet must have come from the rooftop. The bullet went through her heart. I couldn't even scream. I just stared at Sevda - her body lying lifeless. Blood was gushing out her mouth and nose. I couldn't believe it, I couldn't believe she was dying. Her eyes were still looking at me."
Samira says she managed to get Sevda to hospital and she was told they were operating on her, but then the door opened and she saw Sevda had been zipped into a body bag.
Sevda's body was taken away. Samira says it took her days to find her daughter again. Like many others, she found herself at one of Tehran's largest morgues.
"Teenagers - young boys and girls. So many had been killed," she cries.
"I died with every bag I unzipped. I'd never seen so many bodies. But I wouldn't give up."
She finally found her daughter. "Three bodies were piled on top of Sevda. That's how we found her."

Iranian authorities acknowledge that more than 3,000 people were killed in the protests, but claim some were members of the security forces. One human rights group, Hrana, however, estimates the number of dead stands at more than 7,000, most of them protesters.
Finding Sevda's body was just the beginning of Samira's battle with the authorities, she says.
To be allowed to take away the body for burial, she says she was forced to say that "terrorists" rather than the security forces had been responsible for Sevda's death.

"They did this to cover up what they'd done on 8 and 9 January, to hide how many people they had killed. They silenced families by telling them to say their loved ones were killed by Israeli or American terrorists."
Nevertheless she was barred from visiting the grave after the funeral, or organising a tombstone, she says.

And Samira says the harassment continued. A few days before the ceremony to mark 40 days since Sevda died - highly significant in Iranian culture - she says she was summoned by a local branch of the Ministry of Intelligence.

"They told me: 'You should give us an interview and say that Sevda was a Basiji and she was killed by the protesters. Then we will announce her [as] a martyr - you will then receive perks, a house, or anything that you want.'"
She is sure this offer was prompted by fear, because she had shared Sevda's death with an Iranian media organisation based in London, once the internet had been reconnected in the country.
"It scared them that I was in touch with external networks or those outside Iran."
To avoid giving the interview, Samira fled Iran as soon as the 40th day anniversary was over.
"I didn't want to trade with my child's blood."
She says people smugglers helped her to escape. She crossed rivers and mountains to get to safety.
A video she made of herself fleeing makes clear her fury.
"This crap government, these bastards, they've harassed me so much," she tells the camera as she marches along a mountain path bordered by a deep ravine.

Samira says after she continued to give interviews to foreign media from abroad, she was charged in absentia with a string of offences, including "moharebeh" - waging war against God - which can carry the death penalty.
To mark what would have been Sevda's 17th birthday, her relatives and friends held a vigil - with Samira watching from exile on a livestream.
"Then suddenly, the feed cut out," she says.
She discovered that the event had been raided, she says, and some of her family and friends arrested by the IRGC.
She says her family was warned by the authorities that, if they continued to gather at Sevda's grave, her body would be exhumed and moved elsewhere.
Now, Samira shares the names, online, of Iranian security force members and officials she believes were responsible for firing fatal shots during the 8 and 9 January protests she and Sevda joined.
"I want justice to be served for every single person whose name I expose, because they have killed so many young people. My goal is for them to be identified so they can be put on trial," she says.

When one of the men Samira named online was later found dead, a regime supporter offered a $5,000 (£3,732) reward for information about her whereabouts, presuming she was responsible. Iranian state media has since reported the arrest of nine people in connection with the death.
Despite the risks, Samira says she refuses to be silenced.
"Every day and every second without Sevda is very difficult for me. It's like a mother who has lost her heart, who has lost her being, has lost her life…

"But the fact that Sevda is not breathing has made it possible for me to stand on my feet… to think about honouring her life and her path... all those bodies I saw, all those body bags I opened looking for Sevda, they all made me fight the Islamic Republic until my last breath."

articles.title: Most Israelis think settlements policy should change to avoid more sanctions, poll finds
articles.summary:
Survey finds UK government’s decision to impose trade ban was not a decisive factor in how Israelis voted in election

The UK government’s decision to impose a ban on trade in goods from…

blocks.text: The UK government’s decision to impose a ban on trade in goods from illegal settlements was not decisive in how Israelis voted in their general election, but a majority think the Israeli government’s settlements policy should change if it is going to lead to further sanctions, a new poll of Israelis shows.

There had been fierce criticism of the UK foreign secretary Ed Miliband’s decision in September to impose a trade ban and wider sanctions on illegal settlements, with some claiming it would drive Israeli voters into the arms of Benjamin Netanyahu.

A survey last month by Israeli social research group aChord shows overall support for foreign sanctions on violent settlers in the West Bank, but there was little support for the UK’s ban on trade with goods from illegal settlements, with many fearing it would end up being extended across Israel.

The survey is unique in showing how much the tougher line on Israel adopted by Britain and some foreign states was affecting the thinking of Israeli voters, and the extent to which Israelis thought it was a response to Israel’s actions or born of hostility to Israel, or even antisemitism.

The survey showed that three-quarters of supporters of the bloc backing Netanyahu said UK sanctions and trade ban policies towards Israel did not affect their vote at all, and to the small extent that they changed anyone’s vote, they shifted voters both ways, leaving no detectable net effect.

Just over three-quarters of all those surveyed (76) – had heard of the UK government announcement on settlements, even if 18 % had only heard the broad headline. Four-fifths of those that were aware of the announcement knew that the policy applied to the West Bank, and not the whole of Israel.

Israel’s relations with the west were “important or very important” to 60% of the supporters of the Change bloc of parties backing Gadi Eisenkot in deciding their vote. But even then these relationships came fifth in importance in a proffered group of six motives for voting. Only 30% of supporters of the Netanyahu bloc said relations with the west mattered in the same way.

But 71% of voters for the opposition Change bloc said the Israeli government should adapt its settlements policy to avoid an escalation of sanctions. Only 14% of Netanyahu bloc voters agreed, most saying instead that the government should continue the policy “whatever the price”.

A plurality of the public – 50% – said the settlement and construction policy in the West Bank should be adjusted to avoid sanctions escalation and international isolation, with 71% of Eisenkot bloc supporters agreeing to this proposition. Support for a change in the policy is strongest among supporters of the Arab parties.
after newsletter promotion

The finding prompted Hannah Weisfeld, the director of the British-Jewish organisation Yachad, to claim the research “illustrates that the Israeli public certainly recognises that if there is not a policy shift in relation to settlement enterprise, the international community is likely to try to create an incentive to shift things from the outside. If anything, that highlights the importance of UK and other allies taking action that targets the occupation.”

The survey also showed that concerns about foreign sanctions are highest when voters feel they will suffer a high personal price. Only 36% of all those surveyed agreed that the settlement policy should continue even if sanctions on banks that finance construction in illegal settlements led either to higher interest rates, difficulties in transferring money abroad, or using credit cards abroad. The poll suggests that the more people feel they will be damaged personally, the more they oppose the settlement policy.

A majority of all Israelis surveyed (52%) support sanctions on individual violent settlers, so long as the sanctions are imposed only on those acting violently, but 70% of Netanyahu bloc supporters oppose foreign sanctions in all circumstances.

There is much less widespread support for the policy of banning the import of goods from the illegal settlement, with 63% of all those surveyed opposing the ban and 26% either supporting the measure outright, or saying they would if it were underlined that the ban would not apply to goods from outside settlements.

articles.title: Israel has ‘historic’ opportunity to change direction, says leader of Arab coalition
articles.summary:
Yousef Jabareen says he is ready to join forces with opposition bloc to oust Benjamin Netanyahu after winning record number of seats in Knesset

The leader of Israel’s main Palestinian…

blocks.text: The leader of Israel’s main Palestinian coalition, which holds the balance of power after Tuesday’s elections, has said the country is facing a historic opportunity to change direction.
Yousef Jabareen, the head of the Joint List, said he was ready to join forces with the “Change” bloc to oust Benjamin Netanyahu and his far-right coalition, and to wrest control of the Knesset.

Turnout among Arab Israelis (Palestinians with Israeli citizenship, 20% of the population) more than doubled to about 80%, transforming the political landscape. Palestinians in the occupied West Bank and Gaza had no vote.

Jabareen said the first demand of the roughly 840,000 Palestinian Israeli voters was to get rid of the Netanyahu government, and in particular its most extreme members, Itamar Ben-Gvir, the national security minister, and Bezalel Smotrich, the finance minister.

“This has been an awful four years … in all areas of life: in terms of house demolition, criminal gangs within the Arab community without any [intervention] from the police; not allocating the needed resources for our municipalities, for our education, for our youth in general; racism in all areas of life – physical attacks against Arabs, the brutality of the police,” Jabareen told the Guardian in one of his first interviews since the election. “So this has been really a very dangerous period.”

He said the next few days would be critical. Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, is due to summon political leaders as early as Wednesday to canvass their recommendations on who should be given the first chance to form the next government, with no single grouping commanding a clear claim on power.

Netanyahu’s coalition lost its majority, dropping from 68 to 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset. The Change bloc of Zionist parties led by the retired general Gadi Eisenkot has 48 seats, leaving the Arab-Israeli parties as potential kingmakers with a record 19 seats. The Joint List has 11, while the more conservative, Islamist Ra’am has eight.

Eisenkot and his partners have pledged not to form a unity government with Netanyahu, but Eisenkot has also put conditions on any potential coalition with Arab parties: they have to recognise that Israel is a Jewish state, accept conscription, and denounce Hamas as a terrorist organisation.

Ra’am and its leader, Mansour Abbas, have signalled it is ready to join an Eisenkot coalition. The Joint List has no intention of joining such a government, but Jabareen said the coalition was ready to keep it afloat from the outside with tactical voting in the Knesset.

“The conditions that [Eisenkot] speaks of are more relevant for parties who would be in the coalition. We are not planning to be in the coalition … for very clear reasons,” Jabareen said at his family home in the northern city of Umm al-Fahm. “As long as the occupation of our people in the West Bank continues, we cannot be part of a government.

“However, in order to use our political power to get rid of the extreme Netanyahu government, we said that we will consider the possibility of supporting from outside. This is an opportunity to change policies, to change attitudes, including towards the Arab community and towards the Palestinian people.
“This is really a historic moment and I hope that there will be partners within the opposition to go ahead with that. We are thinking that this could be the start of a change.”

blocks.caption: Yousef Jabareen: ‘I hope we can find partners to make to make this change real’

blocks.text: Jabareen, 54, a former law professor and the leader of the socialist Hadash party, has yet to talk to Eisenkot since Tuesday’s elections, but he confirmed that informal discussions among opposition parties were under way.

Forming a new government was unlikely to be straightforward. The party leaders in the Change bloc have to agree on a candidate for prime minister. They would also have to accept partnership with Arab parties, either in coalition or from outside. The rightwing opposition leader, Avigdor Lieberman, is said to be the most resistant. Joint List officials said it was unclear whether partnership with Palestinians really crossed Lieberman’s red lines, or whether he was just holding out for a top cabinet position.

Even before a new government could be formed, Jabareen argued, the 67 opponents of Netanyahu in the new Knesset could use their clear majority to wrest control of legislative power. “That would start by changing the speaker of the Knesset,” he said, adding that the opposition could also take control of the committee that oversees the legislative agenda.

“That could be very crucially important … even before we reach conclusions on the issue of a coalition and a new government,” he said, adding that one of the priorities of the new Knesset should be to repeal laws passed by the outgoing majority that infringed the independence of Israel’s judiciary.
To allow an opposition coalition to oust Netanyahu and function as a minority government, Jabareen made clear it would also have to address deep-seated inequality in Israeli society.

“We have suffered from systemic discrimination for years, so if Eisenkot speaks of change, I believe that the change should come also for our community. We need to be treated equally,” he said. “We also ask for a political horizon. We would like to see the war stopped and the resumption of negotiation with the Palestinian leadership. We would like to see a start of a change.”

The Joint List leader said he was concerned over what Netanyahu might do to keep his grip on power. The prime minister has already made allegations, without evidence, that the Arab parties had used Qatari funds illegally in the election campaign, which Jabareen dismissed as a bid to “delegitimise the political power of the Arab community” and “a dangerous incitement”.
One of Jabareen’s concerns was that the Israeli leader would join Donald Trump in the resumption of war on Iran as a pretext for putting off political transition.
“This is really a critical period,” he said. “There should be a clear voice from the opposition to go against any attempt by him to initiate war … or dictate a new military agenda in Israel.”

articles.title: Almost 200,000 passengers expected at PITX post-Undas
articles.summary: The Parañaque Integrated Terminal Exchange (PITX) is expecting a surge of up to 190,000 passengers on Tuesday, November 3, as travelers return to Metro Manila after the Undas break.

blocks.text: November 2, 2026 | 1:25pm
Passengers flock to the Parañaque Integrated Terminal Exchange.
Edd Gumban / The Philippine STAR

MANILA, Philippines — The Parañaque Integrated Terminal Exchange (PITX) is expecting a surge of up to 190,000 passengers on Tuesday, November 3, as travelers return to Metro Manila after the Undas break.

In an interview with "Unang Hirit" on Monday, November 2, PITX senior corporate affairs officer Kolyn Calbasa said passenger volume could reach between180,000 to 190,000 on Tuesday, as regular commuters join the post-holiday rush.
"We expect the influx tomorrow (November 3) because historically, on November 2, there are fewer passengers because others extended their vacations," Calbasa said in a mix of English and Filipino.

Calbasa added that the terminal is coordinating with government agencies to ensure passenger security and safety and manage congestion ahead of the expected surge. Internal preparations are also underway to ensure sufficient bus availability and timely departures.

Despite expecting nearly 200,000 passengers after the holiday, PITX anticipated fewer travelers heading to the provinces for Undas this year, citing a five-day long weekend in mid-November for the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations Summit
Passengers may also expect travel disruptions, including flight cancellations and schedule adjustments, as road closures and traffic restrictions are implemented ahead of the summit.

articles.title: US envoy reaffirms PH alliance 'stronger than ever' after ASEAN defense meet
articles.summary: United States Ambassador to the Philippines Lee Lipton on Monday reaffirmed Washington"s commitment to Philippine security, describing it as “ironclad” and the two countries" alliance as “stronger…

blocks.text: Published November 2, 2026 1:16pm

United States Ambassador to the Philippines Lee Lipton on Monday reaffirmed Washington’s commitment to Philippine security, describing it as “ironclad” and the two countries’ alliance as “stronger than ever.”
Lipton issued the statement following the ASEAN Defense Ministers’ Meeting-Plus in Cebu, which was attended by US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth.
“I want to reaffirm the United States’ enduring commitment to the Philippines and our shared vision for a peaceful, secure, and prosperous Indo-Pacific,” Lipton said.

He said Hegseth’s frequent engagements with Southeast Asian partners demonstrate the Trump administration’s “determination to strengthen alliances, deepen regional cooperation, and ensure that peace is backed by strength.”
Statement to the People of the Philippines https://t.co/7Lz4p0EJtn— U.S. Ambassador Lee Lipton (@USAmbPH) November 2, 2026
Lipton added that the visits of the US Secretary of War also underscore the importance Washington places on Southeast Asia and its alliance with the Philippines.

“Our commitment to Philippine security is ironclad. With President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., the United States and the Philippines have built a powerful partnership grounded in shared principles, mutual respect, and an unwavering commitment to regional stability,” Lipton said.
“As we mark 75 years of the US-Philippines Mutual Defense Treaty, our message is clear: our alliance is stronger than ever,” he added.

Lipton also emphasized Washington’s long-term commitment to the partnership, particularly its support for defending Philippine sovereignty, protecting the country’s territorial integrity, and upholding freedom of navigation.

Beyond defense cooperation, the US envoy said the security partnership should be matched by an equally strong economic relationship, stressing Washington’s support for the Philippines’ economic development.

“The United States is proud to call the Philippines an ally, partner, and friend. Our relationship is not simply a matter of treaties or shared strategic interests; it is a bond between our peoples that grows stronger every day,” Lipton said.

During the ASEAN-United States Defense Ministers’ Informal Meeting, Hegseth proposed developing a framework for defense cooperation between Washington and ASEAN in recognition of the 50th anniversary of US-ASEAN relations.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: End of Sara Duterte impeachment trial 'possible' in November, says prosecution
articles.summary: The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte could wrap up by the end of November if the defense presents its evidence within 10 full trial days, House lead prosecutor and Batangas Rep.…

blocks.text: Published November 2, 2026 1:02pm

The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte could wrap up by the end of November if the defense presents its evidence within 10 full trial days, House lead prosecutor and Batangas Rep. Gerville Luistro said.

In a statement, Luistro raised the possibility after the House prosecution panel on October 13 dropped three of the four Articles of Impeachment against Duterte, which covered allegations of misuse of confidential funds, bribery and grave threats.
The defense team had originally sought 30 trial days to present its evidence on all four Articles of Impeachment under the pretrial order.
“Posible po na matapos ito bago ang katapusan ng Nobyembre,” Luistro said.
(It’s possible that the trial will conclude before the end of November.)
“We have reason to believe na ito pong 30 trial days na ito ay malaki ang mababawas. Sana kalahati na lang o sampu na lang,” she added.
(We have reason to believe that these 30 trial days will be significantly reduced. Hopefully, only half or 10 days will be needed.)
Luistro, however, said the final trial schedule would remain subject to the approval of the Senate impeachment court and the number of witnesses the defense intends to present.
If the defense requires more than the expected 10 full trial days, the proceedings could extend into December.
“But at any rate, we are all hoping and praying na sana naman bago mag-Pasko ay tapos na ang impeachment trial na ito para magkaroon tayo ng closure, and we can all move on,” Luistro said.
(But at any rate, we are all hoping and praying that the impeachment trial will be over before Christmas so we can have closure, and we can all move on.)
The impeachment trial is currently suspended to give way to Senate committee deliberations on the proposed 2027 national budget.
The Senate impeachment court is scheduled to reconvene on November 9 at 10 a.m.

With the decision to drop three Articles of Impeachment, the prosecution will pursue only Article II, which concerns allegations that Duterte failed to fully declare her assets and divest from business interests, raising questions about her unexplained wealth.

Defense lead counsel Sheila Sison earlier said the move would not affect the defense panel's presentation of evidence, stressing that Duterte should still be allowed to address allegations already presented before the impeachment court.

“That prerogative to withdraw an accusation is not the power to suppress its rebuttal on the part of the respondent. The authority to streamline, or to achieve speed in a trial, is not the authority to diminish due process, or to altogether disregard fundamental rules of fairness," Sison said.
"And the desire to reach a verdict expeditiously can never justify reaching it unfairly,” she added.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Kimi Antonelli makes history as youngest F1 champion
articles.summary: Kimi Antonelli became Formula One's youngest world champion and Italy's first since 1953 when he finished third in Sunday's thrilling and crash-hit Mexico City Grand Prix.

image.caption: Four-time champion Max Verstappen and seven-time champion Lewis Hamilton hoist Kimi Antonelli aloft as a carnival of celebrations began after the Mexico City Grand PrixImage: Eloisa Sanchez/REUTERS

blocks.text: Kimi Antonelli became Formula One's youngest world champion at 20 years and 68 days old on Sunday when he finished third in the Mexico City Grand Prix behind race winner Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton.
The previous recordholder was Germany's Sebastian Vettel, who first became a world champion at age 23 in 2010.
Antonelli is also the first Italian champion since 1953.
"I'm speechless. I’m trying to process what has just happened," said Antonelli after finishing the race.
His parents and sister were there to embrace him when he stepped out of the car.
He was then mobbed by his pit crew.

blocks.caption: Antonelli is also the first Italian champion since 1953Image: Claudia Greco/REUTERS

blocks.text: 'An incredible season'
"It's been an incredible season, and to share this podium with Max ​and Lewis is truly incredible. And looking forward to some more battles in the future," the 20-year-old said.
Antonelli, who secured the title with four races remaining, said the final lap was complicated by the excitement of what he had achieved.

"I think I lost two seconds because I could not see ahead, I think I saw two Ferraris," he said. "It was very special, a lot of memories went through my mind at that moment, and I let it all out after achieving one of my biggest dreams."
Antonelli has now risen to 380 points with four races remaining. Verstappen (261) snuck past Hamilton (259) in the standings, but they will be racing for second the rest of the ​way.

blocks.caption: Antonelli said the final lap was complicated by the excitement of what he had achievedImage: Daniel Becerril/REUTERS

blocks.text: Antonelli started the race in ​fourth and needed to finish ‌ninth or better to secure the championship on Sunday no matter what his peers did.
He had a relatively smooth run, though the race was interrupted by a red flag around Lap ​45 when Valtteri Bottas crashed.
Verstappen, meanwhile, claimed his sixth victory at the Mexico City Grand Prix, further cementing his affinity with the circuit.
After Mexico, F1 will head to Brazil and then to Las Vegas.
The final two Grands Prix are scheduled to be held in Qatar and Abu Dhabi. But it remains uncertain whether they will take place, given the geopolitical instability in the region.

articles.title: South Korea to pour billions into AI
articles.summary: South Korea to spend billions to strengthen the country's technological edge.

image.caption: South Korean President Lee Jae Myung leaves after delivering a budget speech for 2027 at the National Assembly in Seoul.Image: Lee Jin-man/REUTERS

blocks.text: South Korea will pour nearly $16 billion on artificial intelligence and semiconductors, South Korea's President Lee Jae Myung said in his annual budget address to parliament.

"We will invest 21.3 trillion won (€14.3 billion, $15.97 billion), nearly twice ​this year's amount, in AI and the three megaprojects of semiconductors, physical ​AI and ‌AI data centres," Lee said on Monday.
He added that 4.7 trillion won will be invested to bolster "frontier AI development projects, with the aim of achieving world-leading performance for our own AI model, a national strategic asset."
South Korea unveils record budget proposal for 2027
The Lee administration has unveiled a record budget proposal for next year, featuring a 12.8% increase in government spending to 820.9 trillion won (€551.5 billion, $615.62 billion).
The proposal needs parliamentary approval, and Lee's party, the Democratic Party of Korea (DPK), currently holds the majority.
South Korea is Asia's fourth-largest economy and home to two of the world's biggest memory chip makers — Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix.
The AI boom has sent demand for memory chips soaring.
South Korea recorded faster-than-expected economic growth in the third quarter, driven by chip exports and investment.

Exports totaled $930 billion from January to October and are on track to surpass $1 trillion this year, making South Korea the fourth country to achieve the milestone after the United States, China and Germany.

articles.title: PH Red Cross attends to over 8,700 patients during Undas 2026
articles.summary: The Philippine Red Cross (PRC) on Monday said it has attended to 8,721 patients nationwide since October 29 amid the observance of Undas 2026.

blocks.text: Published November 2, 2026 12:48pm
The Philippine Red Cross (PRC) on Monday said it has attended to 8,721 patients nationwide since October 29 amid the observance of Undas 2026.
Based on the PRC's latest operational report as of 9 a.m. on Monday, all 8,721 patients received vital signs monitoring.
The PRC said 359 were classified as minor cases, while 19 were considered major cases.
The minor cases included dizziness, headaches, lacerations, abrasions, insect bites, difficulty breathing, sprains, burns, hypertension, fever, and injuries sustained in motorcycle crashes.
Major cases included chest pain, seizures, suspected stroke, cardiac arrest, heat stroke, and difficulty breathing.
According to the PRC, nine patients were brought to hospitals due to conditions such as stroke, body weakness, loss of consciousness, and hypoglycemia.
A total of 297 welfare assistance services were also provided, including psychological first aid, referrals, tracing services, and the distribution of hot meals and food packs.
Other forms of assistance included wheelchair services for 25 individuals, water provision for 149 people, and the distribution of information and education materials.
For its Undas operations, the PRC deployed 1,977 personnel nationwide, composed of 132 staff members and 1,845 volunteers.
Its deployed assets included 73 ambulances, 404 first aid stations, 131 welfare desks, 45 foot patrols, 32 mobile units, and other service vehicles and equipment.

Cemeteries accounted for the largest number of PRC mobilization areas with 349 deployment points nationwide. Other areas included bus terminals, highways, seaports, beaches, airports, and gas stations.
The PRC's Undas Operation 2026 runs from October 29 to November 3. — Joviland Rita/RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: China says Gibo gave Beijing less than five working days’ notice for ASEAN defense talks
articles.summary: China has accused Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. of blocking its participation in last week’s ASEAN defense talks in Cebu, claiming that the Philippines invited China to join the talks…

blocks.text: November 2, 2026 | 12:19pm
China's Defence Attache to the Philippines Yang Lei attends the 13th ASEAN Defence Ministers’ Meeting-Plus (ADMM-Plus) in Cebu on October 29, 2026.
Eloisa Lopez, pool via AFP

MANILA, Philippines — China has accused Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. of blocking its participation in last week’s ASEAN defense talks in Cebu, claiming that the Philippines invited China to join the talks only after pressure from other Southeast Asian states.

In a statement posted on Facebook late Sunday, November 1, the Chinese Embassy in Manila claimed Teodoro “acted out of personal self-interest” and disregarded the principle of openness and inclusivity of the ASEAN Defense Ministers’ Meeting-Plus (ADMM-Plus), which the Philippines hosted in Cebu on October 28 and 29.

“Only after other ASEAN countries expressed strong opposition to such acts that the Philippines Department of National Defense (DND) reluctantly sent an invitation letter to China on October 22,” the embassy said, adding that the letter was signed by an undersecretary “who was unwilling to even put a date on the letter.”
Philstar.com has reached out to Teodoro for comment. This report will be updated with his response.
The allegation follows remarks by China's defense ministry spokesperson on October 29, who alluded to a "Philippine politician" who allegedly obstructed China's participation in the talks.

During a press conference in Beijing, Zhang Xiaogang told reporters that the Philippines had allowed “a certain self-serving politician to act recklessly” and use its chairmanship to block China’s participation, but he did not name Teodoro.
The embassy said all other ADMM-Plus members received their invitations in late September or early October.

"On October 23, Teodoro said in a press conference that China had been sent notice only the previous day," the embassy said. "It left China fewer than five working days for preparation. China was also required to complete its registration within just two days."
"Under such circumstances, it was virtually impossible to complete the necessary preparation," it added.
At his October 23 briefing, Teodoro said the Philippines had sent an invitation to Beijing through a letter signed by Defense Undersecretary Ignacio Madriaga.
Four days later, DND spokesperson Arsenio Andolong confirmed that an invitation had been sent but China had yet to confirm its representative.
Beijing eventually sent Senior Capt. Yang Lei, its defense attaché in Manila, instead of its defense minister, marking China's lowest level of representation at the forum since its launch in 2010.
Teodoro personally welcomed the other delegation heads at the venue but did not greet Yang, who was instead received by Madriaga.
Teodoro said there should be parity in rank, and that an undersecretary welcoming an attaché was “more than courteous.”
The embassy did not identify which ASEAN countries that had supposedly objected to the Philippines’ handling of the invitation.
Zhang made a similar claim last week, but Teodoro dismissed it as Beijing’s view rather than that of ASEAN.
“So it is China’s position, it is not ASEAN’s position,” Teodoro said at the close of the meetings.

articles.title: ‘I want to slap you around a bit, too’: Victorian magistrate reprimanded over language in court
articles.summary:
Judicial commission finds against Vicky Prapas over a series of comments, including one made when school children were present

  • Get our

blocks.text: A magistrate who told a court user “I want to slap you around a bit, too” has come under fire for her offensive and inappropriate language.
The remark was one of several made by Victorian magistrate Vicky Prapas that the state’s judicial watchdog has found to be inappropriate.
Others included asking someone in court: “Do you reckon the substance is screwing with the way you’re thinking?” and asserting that another person “believes their own bullshit”.
The latter comment was made in the presence of a school group, the judicial commission of Victoria said in its findings last week.
The watchdog opened the investigation after receiving a complaint from Victoria Legal Aid concerning Prapas’ rotation through a Melbourne drug court.

The investigation substantiated a range of allegations, including that the magistrate made threatening or intimidating remarks to legal practitioners when they proposed to make or support complaints against her.
Those comments amounted to a “pattern of victimisation”, the commission found.
Prapas was also found to have made an offensive comment about a person from a marginalised group and made an unprofessional remark about another member of the judiciary.

In the written decision, Prapas acknowledged, among other things, that her conduct in some instances had been “unfiltered and intemperate” and that she would have expressed herself differently with the benefit of hindsight.
But she referred to the unique jurisdiction of a drug court, including that her intention was to promote participant recovery, accountability and community safety within its therapeutic framework.
She said she had reflected carefully on the matters raised, and had taken steps to ensure that her communication remained effective, respectful and less susceptible to misunderstanding.
after newsletter promotion
The watchdog was unable to substantiate some allegations, including that the magistrate demonstrated cultural insensitivity.
In handing down its findings, the commission acknowledged drug court proceedings can warrant “open and frank” discussions.
“However, these features do not displace a judicial officer’s obligation to afford all court users civility and respect,” it said.
The brunt of the complaint was referred to the chief magistrate, Lisa Hannan, with recommendations she counsel Prapas.
The watchdog also recommended Prapas familiarise herself with the commission’s conduct guidelines and attend an educational event within a year.

articles.title: Trump makes fevered campaign push in final weekend before election
articles.summary: The US president rallied in states that Republicans previously won - showcasing how tight Tuesday's elections could be in determining control of Congress.

blocks.text: Trump has been campaigning non-stop across the country ahead of the election - even in areas that were once thought to be safe Republican strongholds.
Throughout the weekend, Trump made the case for his party at rallies in Kansas, Florida and Iowa as well as at tele-rallies for candidates in states including Michigan, Ohio and Pennsylvania.

In previous years, Trump easily won Florida, Iowa and Kansas - once considered reliably Republican states - but the president's visits there in the final days of his election drive highlighted just how competitive these states have become in determining control of Congress.

'I've had people eating cat food': Rising cost of living top of mind for US voters

blocks.text: Trump told supporters he had transformed the country, saying Democrats had left the US in a "dark age" but under his command, "we quickly turned it into the golden age of America".

Trump is facing a backlash over the cost of living. Prices have gone up, particularly for fuel, groceries and health care, since the war in Iran began over eight months ago. At these rallies, Trump appeared to have two aims: to change the subject from those issues and use fear to turn out the Republican vote.

At rallies in Florida and Iowa, he highlighted his policies on trade and immigration and said if Democrats were given power, they would "open the border", "bankrupt your family", "take away your guns" and "mutilate your children". He played video montages of Democrats criticising ICE and supporting transgender rights.
In the room at the rallies, supporters cheered, but there has also been disquiet among some Republicans over Trump's appeal with more moderate voters.

In Alaska, home to another crucial Senate race, a judge on Sunday dismissed an attempt by the Trump administration to delay certifying election results if the Republican incumbent candidate loses due to two candidates appearing on the ballot with the same name.

items: Democrat endorses Republican candidate in key Michigan Senate race as party spat erupts
Judge dismisses Trump administration's lawsuit over two Dan Sullivans in Alaska election
Trump says US voter fraud is 'rampant' - evidence suggests it is extremely rare

blocks.text: In the lead up to the election, Trump and his administration have repeatedly cast doubt on both the credibility and security of the vote, despite evidence showing voter fraud is rare. The justice department has launched investigations or demanded votes be set aside in multiple US states.
The stakes are high for Trump, as midterm election results are seen as a measure of how satisfied Americans are with a president's performance.
In most midterm elections, the party that holds the White House typically loses seats in Congress to the opposing party - meaning Trump's Republican party has the most to lose.

Republicans, who currently hold a slim majority in both the House of Representatives and Senate, don't want to relinquish their party's majority in Congress, as losing any seats would hinder their ability to pass laws and shape policies.

Democrats, however, are keen to gain control from Republicans. Holding a majority would enable them to challenge Trump's agenda, give them investigative powers over his administration, and could also help them showcase their vision for America ahead of the 2028 presidential election.
For lawmakers, it's all about gaining or maintaining power and control, but it's Americans who will feel the impacts of their policies.

Who gets elected at the city, state, and federal level affects many aspects of voters' everyday lives, including the cost of gas, rising inflation and grocery prices, healthcare and abortion access, income and property taxes, and immigration.

articles.title: China state broadcaster pulls La Liga matches following Mbappé joke
articles.summary: China Media Group, which acknowledged Mbappé's apology, has not said how long the blackout will last.

blocks.text: China's state broadcaster CCTV did not air a Real Madrid match on Sunday, despite the club's star striker Kylian Mbappé's apology for his "ill-judged" remarks on the late Chinese leader Mao Zedong.
Mbappé drew huge backlash after saying the meme "that makes [him] laugh the most" was the one in which his face is superimposed on a "Chinese dictator" resembling Mao.

China Media Group, CCTV's parent organisation, said last Tuesday it would suspend broadcasts of Spanish football La Liga matches following the furore, which also led to Mbappé being dropped by several Chinese brands.
China's foreign ministry had said it took Mbappé's apology "seriously". Real Madrid and La Liga have also apologised.
China Media Group had earlier demanded apologies from the three parties, calling them "an absolute prerequisite" for moving past the incident.
It has acknowledged the apologies, but has not commented on how long the broadcast blackout will last.
Mbappé, who reportedly made his remark about the meme on French talk show The Bridge, apologised later on Tuesday.
"My comment was ill-judged, and I now understand that it hurt many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world," he had said.
The joke did not go down well in China, where Mao is revered by the Communist Party, despite his having overseen one of the bloodiest chapters in the country's past.
Mao, who led the Chinese Communist Party to victory in the civil war and founded the People's Republic of China, died in 1976.
During his rule he oversaw the Great Leap Forward and the Cultural Revolution, which led to a famine that killed tens of millions and unleashed violent purges across Chinese society.
This is not the first time Beijing has suspended sports broadcasts over political sensitivities.

It pulled NBA games for a year from October 2019 after Daryl Morey, the general manager of Houston Rockets, tweeted in support of Hong Kong protesters during widespread pro-democracy protests in the city.
Morey backtracked on his comment after fierce criticism from Chinese fans, sponsors and commercial partners.
"I have had a lot of opportunity since that tweet to hear and consider other perspectives," Morey later wrote.
"I have always appreciated the significant support our Chinese fans and sponsors...I would hope that those who are upset will know that offending or misunderstanding them was not my intention."
Real Madrid beat Racing Santander 3-0 in Sunday's match, with goals from Mbappé, Jude Bellingham and Yan Diomande.

articles.title: Binance users withdraw $3.6bn after largest-ever crypto hack
articles.summary: The exchange froze transactions following the incident which has been linked to a North Korean group.

blocks.text: Binance customers withdrew $3.6bn (£2.7bn) of assets from the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange as it reopened on Sunday following what is believed to be the largest hack in history.
The firm suspended all transactions in the wake of the incident, which impacted $6.3bn worth of digital assets.
Major organisations, including the US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), have accused North Korea of being responsible for the cyber-attack.

The company said it has covered around 95% of the assets stolen in the breach but the remaining amount may take longer to source. Binance has repeatedly said it would cover all of the losses linked to the attack.
Binance said on X: "Between 06:00 and 15:30 [GMT] on November 1, we processed $4.649 billion in withdrawals and $1.01 billion in deposits, resulting in a net outflow of approximately $3.64 billion."
There was an "initial spike" in withdrawals, which later declined and "are stabilising as expected", it added.
Sunday's net withdrawals account for just over 2% of the $171bn of assets under its management, said Binance.
The firm said last week that it has reserved more than $6.3bn in funds, to deal with ​the fallout of the attack.
Binance also said withdrawals of more than two dozen major cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin and Ethereum have resumed and that more services will resume in phases once security checks are completed.

articles.title: PNP conducts operation vs Bantag at Ifugao poultry farm
articles.summary: The Philippine National Police (PNP) on Monday said an operation was conducted to arrest former Bureau of Corrections (BuCor) chief Gerald Bantag at a poultry farm in Barangay Pugol, Lamut, Ifugao on…

blocks.text: Published November 2, 2026 11:29am

The Philippine National Police (PNP) on Monday said an operation was conducted to arrest former Bureau of Corrections (BuCor) chief Gerald Bantag at a poultry farm in Barangay Pugol, Lamut, Ifugao on Sunday.
However, Bantag was not found at the location during the operation.

“Police conducted an operation at a poultry farm in Barangay Pugol, Lamut, Ifugao on November 1 after receiving information that Bantag was hiding there and posing as a poultry worker,” the PNP said in a statement.
“However, he was not found at the location,” it added.
The PNP said it remains committed to pursuing Bantag, who is wanted over his alleged involvement in the 2022 killing of broadcaster Percival Mabasa or "Percy Lapid."
PNP chief Police General Jose Melencio C. Nartatez Jr. said authorities would continue their efforts to serve the warrant against Bantag.
“We will not allow the passage of time or repeated attempts to evade arrest to weaken our resolve. The PNP will remain relentless in pursuing those who are wanted by the law,” Nartatez said.
“Every lead will be pursued, every lawful opportunity will be acted upon, and we will not stop until they are brought before the courts to answer for the charges against them,” he added.
Nartatez described the recent operation as proof of the police force's determination to locate and arrest wanted individuals.
“This is not a setback but a proof that we remain relentless in locating and arresting him as well as other high-profile fugitives,” he said.
The PNP also called on the public to provide information that could help authorities locate Bantag and other wanted individuals.

In April 2023, a Muntinlupa Regional Trial Court court ordered the arrest of Bantag in connection with the death of Jun Villamor, the alleged middleman in the killing of broadcaster Percy Lapid in October 2022.
Bantag has denied the allegations against him.
The Department of Justice (DOJ) previously said a P2-million reward would be given for information leading to Bantag’s arrest. — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: Bantag allegedly disguised as poultry worker, not found during Ifugao police operation
articles.summary: Fugitive former Bureau of Corrections Chief Gerald Bantag has eluded arrest in Ifugao, according to the mayor of Lamut, Ifugao.

blocks.text: November 2, 2026 | 11:19am
The place where former Bureau of Corrections Chief Gerald Bantag allegedly eluded arrest on the early morning of Nov. 1, 2026.
Mariano B. Buyagawan Jr. / Facebook
MANILA, Philippines — Fugitive former Bureau of Corrections Chief Gerald Bantag has eluded arrest in Ifugao, according to the mayor of Lamut, Ifugao.
In a Facebook post, Lamut Mayor Mariano Buyagawan Jr. said Bantag was hiding at a local poultry farm, where he allegedly disguised himself as a poultry worker.

“So what is a fugitive General doing? He was not hiding in the mountains. Not in a cave. Not in another country. He was hiding inside the poultry farm in Pugol! Wearing slippers! Holding a balde (bucket) of chicken feeds! Pretending to be a poultry boy!” Buyagawan said in a Facebook post on Sunday, November 1.
According to Buyagawan, police raided the farm at 5 a.m. on Sunday.
The Police Regional Office - Cordillera (PRO-CAR) also confirmed that an operation to arrest Bantag had been conducted.
PRO-CAR said that the operation was carried out by personnel from the Ifugao PPO and the 1501st Regional Mobile Force Battalion 15.
“However, the operation yielded no arrest, as the subject of the warrant was not present in the area during implementation,” the PRO-CAR said.
However, contrary to Buyagawan’s claim, PRO-CAR said Bantag did not evade arrest because he was not present in the area during the operation.

“PRO-CAR clarifies that no arrest was made because the subject was not present at the identified location when police personnel conducted the operation. Thus, the claim that the subject eluded arrest is not true,” it said.
Police urged the public “to remain vigilant and cooperate with law enforcement authorities by providing credible information that may help locate wanted persons.”

Bantag is facing murder charges in connection with the killings of broadcaster Percy Lapid and inmate Jun Villamor, as well as corruption-related complaints over the alleged misuse of funds for prison projects.
His alleged accomplice, Denver Mayores, was sentenced to two to eight years in prison for his role in Lapid’s killing.

articles.title: Nine killed as small jet crashes on Florida street
articles.summary: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy described the crash, which happened near President Trump's Mar-a-Lago resort, as a "horrific tragedy".

blocks.text: US media reports and flight analysis indicate that the jet was plummeting hundreds of feet per second before crashing.

In air traffic control audio recorded moments before the crash, the pilot of the aircraft can be heard saying the plane was descending 10,000 feet per minute, according to the BBC's US partner CBS News.
Then the pilot declared an emergency, yelling, "We are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000 feet per minute," CBS reported.
"We're gonna crash ... We're out of time," the pilot told the tower.

Unverified footage posted on social media shows what appears to be a dash-camera recording of the moment of the crash. It shows vehicles driving on a residential suburban street, when suddenly an aircraft nosedives into the ground almost vertically, and explodes into a large fireball.

"When you see that video, it's a jarring thing," Florida Governor Ron DeSantis told reporters at a news conference after the crash. "It's like a missile coming down, and a massive explosion, debris going everywhere."
It is not yet clear who was aboard the jet when it crashed. DeSantis said "as of now, we don't have any reports of anyone who was on the ground...who was killed or injured".
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy described the crash as a "horrific tragedy", and said the FAA was sending a team to the scene to help an investigation by the National Transportation Safety Board.
"Please join me in praying for the families and loved ones of those we lost," Duffy added.
Palm Beach County Fire Rescue has declared a "mass casualty incident".

articles.title: Bicam talks on 2027 budget to be opened to CSOs -- JV Ejercito
articles.summary: Senate finance committee chairperson JV Ejercito has committed to inviting civil society organizations (CSOs) to observe the bicameral conference committee deliberations on the proposed P7.2-trillion…

blocks.text: Published November 2, 2026 10:31am

Senate finance committee chairperson JV Ejercito has committed to inviting civil society organizations (CSOs) to observe the bicameral conference committee deliberations on the proposed P7.2-trillion national budget for fiscal year 2027.

Just like last year, Ejercito also confirmed that the bicameral deliberations which would reconcile the Senate and the House of Representatives’ differing versions of the budget bill, would also be livestreamed to allow the public to watch the proceedings in real time.
“We are continuing to build on our best practices. This year, we will be inviting CSOs to sit in and observe the bicameral proceedings,” the senator said in a statement.
“Having more eyes on the budget will help us spot any unvetted projects or last-minute insertions that may be introduced during the bicam,” he added.
Last Monday, October 26, the Senate panel conducted a dedicated hearing with CSOs to discuss their recommendations and concerns on the 2027 budget.

During the hearing, the People's Budget Coalition (PBC) cautioned against over a trillion worth of “red flags” under the proposed budget. These reportedly covered various types of “pork” or discretionary funds under the House General Appropriations Bill (GAB).

House leaders, on the other hand, defended the amendments made by the chamber to the proposed 2027 national budget, saying these were purportedly based on agency proposals and had been made on valid grounds.
Ejercito maintained that he wants to ensure that every single peso in the 2027 budget would be “accountably and transparently allocated.”
He also invited the public to use the digital tools developed by CSOs in reviewing budget documents and flagging questionable allocations.

“Transparency is not just a policy statement, it is an active mechanism. These tools were built by watchdogs themselves, and we are glad to give them a home on the Senate website so ordinary citizens can scrutinize where public funds are going,” Ejercito said.
The Senate Finance panel is currently finalizing its committee report, with Ejercito set to formally sponsor the 2027 General Appropriations Bill on the floor this month. — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: Police use facial recognition to scan one million faces in WA trial leading to 122 arrests
articles.summary:
Deployments of surveillance vans over five months result in nine false alerts and led officers to engage with 146 registered sex offenders

  • Get our

blocks.text: More than a million people have had their faces scanned in a trial of real-time facial recognition technology in Western Australia, resulting in 122 arrests and nine incorrect alerts.
WA police said under the five-month trial, which concluded on Saturday, the technology scanned 1,380,882 faces after 100 deployments across 43 regional and metropolitan locations.
Alongside the 122 arrests, the alerts led officers to engage with 146 registered sex offenders and locate 10 people for a welfare check.
The deployments included three operations at the Perth Royal Show, where 223,749 faces were scanned, resulting in 15 alerts, three arrests and seven “interactions” with registered sex offenders.
A police spokesperson confirmed the system generated nine incorrect alerts against the total 1.38m scans, meaning there was an error rate of 0.00065%.
Addressing the false matches at a media conference on Sunday, the WA police commissioner, Col Blanch, confirmed officers engaged with each individual.
“I want to be very clear on those false alerts,” he said. “No one was arrested. No one made a complaint. Each one did result in an interaction with that person and asking them relevant questions.

“It’s a very, very, very low number. It’s not zero. We’d love it to be zero. But I think the important thing for us is to engage with our community just like we would if a human thought someone was a wanted person.”

Blanch acknowledged the technology was “not perfect” and that authorities “knew this going into this trial”, but maintained that officers followed up on alerts in the same way they would if a member of the public raised suspicions.
However, civil liberties advocates have criticised how the WA police framed the error rate.

The chief executive of Civil Liberties Australia, Bill Rowlings, said WA police were “severely gilding the lily” by claiming the incorrect alert rate was 0.00065% and suggested it should instead be calculated by comparing how many of the arrests resulted in convictions.
“We will only know what the incorrect rate is when the 122 people arrested have their day in court,” he said.
after newsletter promotion
“If half the 122 arrested … are not convicted, the ‘incorrect’ rate will be 50%,” he said in a statement, saying police had performed the almost 1.4m scans “with no reasonable suspicion whatsoever”.

When the trial was announced, the state’s independent privacy watchdog, the Office of the Information Commissioner WA (OIC WA), said it was not involved in implementing the trial, warning of “collective privacy harms” in a statement. The OIC WA was contacted for comment.

blocks.caption: The police surveillance vans have now been removed from public deployment while the trial is evaluated. Photograph: Aaron Bunch/AAP

blocks.text: On Sunday, Blanch said the trial “focused on using modern technology responsibly to identify people who presented a risk, while allowing the vast majority of people to go about their day without any impact”.

Under the trial guidelines, cameras mounted on or positioned near marked police vehicles scanned faces in designated public areas, matching them against an alert list drawn from police databases. Police said images of people who weren’t on the list were pixelated in real time and deleted immediately without being stored.

The trial previously triggered backlash over concerns about privacy and algorithmic bias. Experts say the technology could disproportionately affect marginalised groups who are already overrepresented on police watchlists, with facial recognition algorithms historically having higher false-match rates for people with darker skin tones.

The surveillance vans have now been removed from public deployment while the force conducts an internal evaluation into how the technology performed on the ground and its community impacts, including “reviewing the safeguards and whether all requirements were met”.

articles.title: German police investigating after needles found in Halloween candy
articles.summary: German police said they received phone calls with reports about sharp objects concealed in Halloween candy.

image.caption: Police are investigating reports about foreign objects in Halloween candyImage: Polizei Hannover/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Needles or other sharp metal objects have been found in sweets that children collected while trick-or-treating for Halloween, German police said Sunday.
Police believe most or all of the objects, which also included metal screws, were placed intentionally to cause harm.
Incidents were reported in Thuringia, Baden-Württemberg, Bavaria, Lower Saxony, and Rhineland-Palatinate, among other locations, police said.
In one of the cases in the southern city of Nuremberg, police said a child had bitten down on a needle while eating a piece of chocolate. The child was unharmed.
In two separate cases in the southwestern state of Baden-Württemberg, police said the needles had been concealed as such that they were not visible from the outside.
In several of the cases, police have opened investigations into attempted aggravated assault.

articles.title: Spain train crash: US, Japan and Canada citizens among dead, authorities say
articles.summary:
The train disaster, one of Europe’s deadliest rail incidents this century, killed 69 people, including 54 Spaniards

Four US citizens and one each from Canada, Japan, Argentina, Mexico,…

blocks.text: Four US citizens and one each from Canada, Japan, Argentina, Mexico, Tunisia and the Czech Republic were among the 69 killed in last week’s high-speed train collision in Spain, authorities said.

Wednesday’s disaster – one of Europe’s deadliest rail accidents this century – has seen victims’ relatives endure an agonising wait as forensics teams identify the dead, sometimes from individual body parts.
A legal body set up to handle the identification work, made up of police and forensics experts, announced in a statement late on Sunday the 10 latest confirmed foreign victims.
It had already announced the deaths of a French and a Portuguese citizen, as well as that of 54 Spaniards.
All but three of the victims are now identified, the statement added.
Three reports for missing people remain active, the authorities said. They concern two Australians and one Japanese citizen.
“As the contacted families have expressed their wish to travel to Spain to carry out in-person identification, we are awaiting their arrival in the country,” the statement said.

The accident was Spain’s second high-speed train collision this year and raised fresh questions about the country’s rail safety, after a crash in the southern region of Andalusia in January killed 46 people.

The latest disaster struck when a service by state operator Renfe ploughed into the back of a stationary train belonging to Spanish company Iryo outside the central village of Urda, around 130km (80 miles) south of Madrid.
The failure of an automatic safety system halted all trains on a 63km stretch of track, but a control centre authorised the Renfe service to resume its journey while the other train was still.
The tragedy came one month before a 29 November general election in which Socialist leader Pedro Sánchez will seek to overcome unfavourable polls and extend his eight-year premiership.

articles.title: Democrats have high hopes for midterms, but polls have let them down before
articles.summary: Polls have been predicting a Democratic surge, but last-minute deciders and sampling issues mean there's no guarantee.

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
By
North America correspondent
The Democratic Party has high expectations as it heads into these pivotal US midterm elections.
A historically unpopular Republican president, an American public unhappy with the rising costs of food and bills, and months of favourable polls point to a good night for them on Tuesday.

Democratic candidates lead in well over the 218 seats needed to flip control of the lower chamber of Congress, the House of Representatives, the polls suggest. And they are tied or narrowly ahead in the key Senate races.

A recent New York Times poll had the Senate race in South Carolina, a state Donald Trump won by 18 percentage points in 2024, as a tie. Recent CNN surveys put the Democrats ahead in Texas, Kansas and Maine.
But are the polls accurate?

Recent US political history is littered with examples where public opinion polls, even ones just days before an election, were off the mark. Trump outperformed predictions on his way to White House victories in 2016 and 2024. His narrow defeat in 2020 came after most surveys indicated a more comfortable win for Democrat Joe Biden.

Earlier this year, polls suggested Democrat Abdul El-Sayed was poised for a double-digit win in Michigan's Democratic Senate primary. Instead it was 1%. In Wisconsin's Democratic primary for governor, the candidate that had a polling lead that approached 20 points lost by a fraction of a percent.

According to Clifford Young, president of Ipsos Public Affairs, which conducts political and market research surveys, polling has become difficult in recent years because it's harder to reach Americans as they abandon their land lines and screen their calls. And many of those who pollsters do contact have become less willing to participate.
"Conservatives, especially those on the far right, are much more anti-establishment by nature," Young says. "And they don't participate in anything. They hate the system. That's the challenge."

If Republican voters are being undercounted in a systematic way, and polling companies don't take that into consideration when constructing their voting models, it could skew their data towards the Democrats.
That's one of the reasons why it has become trickier for pollsters to predict what the electorate will look like.
What's at stake for Trump in the US midterms?
In recent years, midterm general election polls have proven to be more accurate, in part because Trump - and his unique ability to draw disaffected Americans to the polls - was not on the ballot.
In 2022, they suggested Democrats would defy conventional expectations and avoid an electoral wipe-out despite Biden's low approval numbers.
While the party lost control of the House of Representatives, the margins were slim and Democrats maintained control of the US Senate.

While this year's primary results did provide bigger surprises, Young says that nominating contests have historically been volatile, with voters more likely to make up their minds at the last minute. It shouldn't be seen as an indication that the current crop of general election polls are off the mark.
It's common for the party of the president to have a bad night in the midterms.
One of the most notable examples in recent years came in 2010 when Republicans flipped more than 60 House seats and made gains in the Senate.

It came off the back of an economy struggling to recover from the financial crash and conservative fears over President Barack Obama's healthcare reforms. A defeat had been predicted by the polls but not quite on that scale.

The roles are reversed this time, with the Democrats in opposition and the economy on the minds of voters. But there are a number of reasons why Democrats may not have as good a night as history might suggest or as some might expect, given Trump's low approval rating.
Firstly, much of the territory in play in this election Trump conquered with ease in the presidential election just two years ago. It's like a home game for Republicans.
Then there have been changes to House election boundaries over the years that have meant fewer seats switch between parties.
Thirdly, there are fewer swing voters due to the deeper polarisation of the country. Some experts describe the electorate as calcified.
There's also the cash advantage Republicans have enjoyed which has given them hundreds of millions of dollars to spend on attack ads in the final weeks.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Obama gives a press conference the day after the heavy 2010 midterms defeat

blocks.text: Obama gives a press conference the day after the heavy 2010 midterms defeat
Polling models try to capture shifting fundamentals. And a well-designed poll is built to anticipate issues that may make it less than reliable.

Individual polls do have a built-in margin of error – a statistical level of uncertainty based on the sampling size compared to the population as a whole. Taken as an aggregate, polling averages and not individual surveys can provide a more accurate prediction.

At the moment, even the kind of polling lean we saw in recent presidential elections would suggest Democrats are likely to have a good night on 3 November. And polling inaccuracies can go both ways. In last year's state and special elections, Democrats outperformed most surveys as it was their voters who turned out in unexpectedly larger numbers.

The sight of Trump holding rallies in the final days of the campaign in states he won comfortably in 2024 will have lifted Democrats' hopes that Republican internal polling has conservative candidates in trouble.
Voter voices: What issues matter most to Americans?
There's always the chance that voters change their minds right up until election day, however.

Sometimes there are late shifts that can alter the dynamics of a race. Sometimes undecided voters, which still account for a key segment of the electorate in many of these races, all break the same way.
In polling, there will always be some level of uncertainty – and managing that is the art that goes along with the science.
"I think we're doing a better job," says Young. "But part of the problem we always have is not just with the pollsters. Part of it is that we're dealing with humans. Humans are not easy."
